documents.title: Atlas platform end-to-end architecture
documents.summary: Deep-dive into how Atlas services, data stores, event streams and the ops console fit together.
documents.body:
This is the reference picture of Atlas as it runs in production in us-east-1. It is written for new engineers and for agents who need to reason about blast radius before changing anything. Keep it updated when a service is added or a data flow changes.

## Repositories

Application code lives in the monorepo `github.com/northwind/atlas`. The layout is:

- `services/<name>` — one directory per Go service (`dispatch-svc`, `tracking-svc`, `billing-svc`, `rate-engine`, `notify-svc`, `docs-svc`, `atlas-gateway`, `outbox-relay`, `edi-bridge`).
- `web/ops-console` — the TypeScript/React operator UI.
- `ml/eta-predictor` — the Python ETA service plus training pipelines.
- `cmd/atlasctl` — the internal operator CLI, used by most runbooks.
- `proto/` — shared protobuf definitions, linted with `buf`.

Infrastructure is in a separate repo, `github.com/northwind/atlas-infra`, applied through Atlantis. Nothing in the app monorepo is allowed to create AWS resources.

## Request path

External traffic (shipper portals, carrier apps, the ops console) enters through CloudFront and an ALB into `atlas-gateway` on port 8080. The gateway terminates JWTs issued by Okta (for humans) or by the partner-token service (for integrations), applies per-client rate limits (600 requests per minute by default) and translates REST calls into gRPC calls to the internal services. Inside the cluster every hop is mTLS via Linkerd, so services never deal with certificates directly.

The ops console itself is a static bundle on S3 behind CloudFront; it talks only to the gateway.

## Core services

- **dispatch-svc** (HTTP 8081, gRPC 50051) owns loads, tenders and carrier assignment. It is the heart of the business: if dispatch is down, freight does not move. Its database is `dispatch`.
- **rate-engine** (HTTP 8084, gRPC 50054) prices lanes. Dispatch calls it synchronously when building a tender, and the quote is cached in Redis.
- **tracking-svc** (HTTP 8082, gRPC 50052) ingests GPS pings from trucks and ELD providers, computes geofence arrivals, and stores the time series in `tracking.gps_pings`.
- **billing-svc** (HTTP 8083) turns delivered loads into invoices and keeps the append-only ledger in `billing.ledger_events`.
- **notify-svc** (HTTP 8086) sends SMS, email and push notifications to drivers and shippers.
- **docs-svc** (HTTP 8087) stores bills of lading and proof-of-delivery images in S3 bucket `nwf-atlas-docs-prod`.
- **eta-predictor** (Python/FastAPI on 9400) predicts arrival times for in-flight loads.
- **edi-bridge** translates EDI 204/990/214 messages from large carriers into Atlas API calls.

All Go services expose Prometheus metrics on port 9090 at `/metrics` and health on `/healthz` (liveness) and `/readyz` (readiness).

## Data stores

Each service owns its own Postgres database on a shared Aurora PostgreSQL 15 cluster (see ADR-003). Services never read another service's tables; they consume events instead. Connections in production go through PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode, which matters for anyone writing code that uses session-level features like advisory locks or `SET` statements.

Redis (ElastiCache, cluster mode) is used for three things only: the rate-quote cache, the ETA feature cache, and ops-console sessions. It is never a system of record; losing Redis must degrade latency, not correctness.

## Events

Kafka on Amazon MSK is the event backbone (ADR-005). The most important topics are:

- `dispatch.load-events.v1` — every load and tender state transition.
- `telemetry.gps.v2` — raw pings, 48 partitions, keyed by `truck_id`.
- `billing.ledger.v1` — ledger postings produced by billing and consumed by the finance warehouse.
- `notify.requests.v1` — notification requests from any service.
- `eta.predictions.v1` — ETA outputs, consumed by dispatch and the console.

Services do not publish directly inside a business transaction. They write to an `outbox_events` table in the same transaction and `outbox-relay` forwards rows to Kafka (ADR-009). This is why you will see a few hundred milliseconds of delay between a database write and the corresponding event.

## A load's lifecycle, end to end

1. A shipper creates a load through the gateway; dispatch-svc persists it in `dispatch.loads` and emits `LoadCreated`.
2. Dispatch asks rate-engine for a price on the lane, then offers a tender to one or more carriers. A tender expires after `dispatch.tender.expiry_seconds` (600 seconds).
3. When a carrier accepts, dispatch writes `dispatch.load_assignments` and emits `TenderAccepted`. notify-svc picks up the notification request and texts the driver.
4. As the truck moves, tracking-svc consumes pings, detects geofence entry at pickup and delivery, and emits `StopArrived` / `StopDeparted`.
5. eta-predictor consumes load and tracking events, refreshes the prediction, and publishes to `eta.predictions.v1`. If the model is unavailable, a rules-based fallback is used and error code ATL-5500 is logged.
6. On delivery, docs-svc receives the POD image; billing-svc sees `LoadDelivered` plus the POD reference and creates an invoice in `billing.invoices`.

## Failure domains

The key thing to understand is which dependencies are synchronous. Dispatch depends synchronously on rate-engine and Postgres. Everything else is asynchronous through Kafka, which means an outage in billing, notify or eta-predictor causes lag, not user-facing errors. In practice that makes consumer lag the single most important signal to watch for the async half of the platform, and the "Atlas / Kafka Consumer Lag" Grafana dashboard is the first place on-call looks.

## Where to go next

- Tracking ingestion internals: see the tracking pipeline deep-dive memory.
- ETA model serving: see the eta-predictor architecture memory.
- Ports, hosts and env vars: see the environment memories.
- The tender state machine and idempotency rules are documented separately because they come up in code review constantly.

One last detail that surprises people: the DR region is us-west-2, run as a warm standby (ADR-023). Only the Aurora global database replica and the MSK mirror are running there continuously; EKS workloads in us-west-2 are scaled to zero and come up during a regional failover exercise. The recovery time objective agreed with the business is 60 minutes, and the recovery point objective is 5 minutes.

documents.title: How GPS telemetry flows through tracking-svc
documents.summary: Detailed walkthrough of GPS ping ingestion, deduplication, geofencing and storage in tracking-svc.
documents.body:
Written after INC-2025-031 by Marcus Oyelaran so that the next person debugging tracking lag does not have to reverse-engineer the pipeline from code. It covers what happens between a truck sending its position and the ops console drawing a dot on the map.

## Sources of pings

Pings arrive from three places:

1. **ELD provider webhooks** (Samsara, Motive and a long tail of smaller vendors). Each provider has an adapter in `services/tracking-svc/internal/providers/`. Adapters normalise vendor payloads into the `atlas.telemetry.v2.Ping` protobuf.
2. **The Northwind driver app**, which posts batches every 30 seconds while a load is active.
3. **edi-bridge**, for carriers that still send EDI 214 status messages. These are low-resolution (city-level) and flagged `source=EDI` so the map can draw them differently.

All three paths end at the same place: the webhook handlers do minimal validation and publish to the Kafka topic `telemetry.gps.v2`. They never write to Postgres directly. This keeps the HTTP endpoints fast even during a database incident.

## The topic

`telemetry.gps.v2` has 48 partitions, replication factor 3, and 72 hours of retention. Messages are keyed by `truck_id`, which guarantees per-truck ordering. The v1 topic keyed by `load_id` was retired in March 2025 because a truck carrying multiple LTL loads produced out-of-order updates across partitions. Peak volume is roughly 38,000 messages per second on weekday mornings Eastern time, and the average message is about 310 bytes.

## The ingest consumer

The consumer group is `tracking-ingest`. It runs as the `tracking-ingest` deployment (separate from the tracking-svc API deployment) with 24 replicas in production, so each pod normally owns two partitions. The Kafka client is franz-go. After the rebalance storm in July 2025, the group uses the cooperative-sticky assignor with `session.timeout.ms=45000` and `max.poll.interval.ms=300000`; do not lower those without reading the INC-2025-031 postmortem.

For each batch the consumer:

1. **Deduplicates** using a Redis set per truck with a 10-minute TTL. Vendors resend pings on retry, and roughly 4% of traffic is duplicate.
2. **Validates** coordinates and timestamps. Pings older than `tracking.ping.stale_after` (15 minutes) relative to receive time are still stored but marked stale, and error code ATL-5031 is logged at debug level. A burst of ATL-5031 almost always means a vendor is replaying a backlog, not that our pipeline is slow.
3. **Snaps** to the active load. The truck-to-load mapping is read from a local cache that is refreshed from `dispatch.load-events.v1`.
4. **Evaluates geofences** for the load's stops. Geofences are circles with a default radius of 400 metres (configurable per facility). Entry requires two consecutive pings inside the fence to avoid GPS jitter creating false arrivals.
5. **Writes** a batch insert into `tracking.gps_pings` using `COPY` for throughput.
6. **Emits** `StopArrived` and `StopDeparted` events via the outbox when a geofence transition is confirmed.

Offsets are committed only after the Postgres write succeeds. That means a Postgres slowdown shows up as consumer lag, which is the intended behaviour: we would rather lag than drop pings.

## Storage

`tracking.gps_pings` is range-partitioned by day on `recorded_at` using pg_partman (see ADR-012). Partitions are pre-created seven days ahead by the `partman-maintenance` CronJob and dropped after 90 days. Queries that do not include a `recorded_at` predicate will scan every partition, and the Aurora reader will complain loudly; the console's map endpoint always bounds the window to the load's active period.

Indexes per partition: `(truck_id, recorded_at DESC)` and a BRIN index on `recorded_at`. There is deliberately no index on `load_id` in the ping table; the load association is stored in `tracking.load_track_segments`, which is much smaller.

## Serving the map

The ops console asks the gateway for `/v1/loads/{id}/track`. tracking-svc answers from `tracking.load_track_segments` plus the last 30 minutes of raw pings, downsampled with Douglas-Peucker to at most 500 points. Live updates reach the console through a server-sent events stream at `/v1/loads/{id}/track/stream`, which is fed from an in-memory fan-out inside the tracking-svc API pods.

## What to watch

- Grafana "Atlas / Tracking Ingest": ingest rate, dedupe ratio, geofence events per minute, COPY latency.
- Grafana "Atlas / Kafka Consumer Lag": group `tracking-ingest`. The page threshold is 500,000 messages of lag sustained for 10 minutes.
- The metric `atlas_tracking_pings_stale_total` split by provider.

## Known sharp edges

- A single truck that sends a huge backlog (we have seen 200,000 pings from one misconfigured tablet) will pin one partition. Lag on one partition only is a signal of this, not of a cluster problem.
- GC pauses above a few seconds used to trigger rebalances. The pods now run with `GOMEMLIMIT` set to 90% of the container limit (the container limit is 1.5 GiB).
- The geofence evaluator depends on the dispatch event stream. If `dispatch.load-events.v1` is lagging, new loads will not be matched and pings land with `load_id = NULL`. They are re-associated by the nightly `atlasctl tracking reassociate` job, but arrivals for that period will be late.

## Capacity numbers worth remembering

- Each `tracking-ingest` pod sustains about 2,200 pings per second before COPY latency starts climbing, so 24 pods give roughly 40% headroom over the weekday peak. The HPA can scale to 48 pods, but more pods than partitions is pointless: pods 49 and beyond would sit idle.
- The `tracking` database grows by roughly 22 GB per day of raw pings before compression. With 90-day retention that is the single largest consumer of Aurora storage, which is why the retention window is guarded by ADR-012 rather than being a casual config change.
- The SSE fan-out in the API pods is sized for about 3,000 concurrent console viewers. During peak season the dispatch floor alone has around 400 users, so there is plenty of room, but a runaway browser tab that reconnects in a loop can still show up as a spike in `atlas_tracking_sse_connections`.

## History

- v1 of the pipeline (2024) wrote pings directly from webhook handlers into Postgres. It fell over during the first peak season, which is where the "never write from the webhook" rule comes from.
- The move to `telemetry.gps.v2` keyed by truck happened in March 2025 (ticket ATLAS-1187).
- The cooperative-sticky assignor and the new timeouts came from INC-2025-031 in July 2025 (ticket ATLAS-1642).

The operational side (how to actually drain lag) lives in the tracking consumer-lag runbook, not here.

documents.title: ETA predictor service design and model serving
documents.summary: Architecture of the Python eta-predictor: feature building, model serving, fallback and publishing.
documents.body:
The eta-predictor lives in `ml/eta-predictor` and is owned by Farah Nadeem's ML team. It is the only Python service in the production request path, and it is built so that the rest of Atlas does not notice when it misbehaves.

## Components

There are three deployables:

1. **eta-feature-builder** — a Kafka consumer (group `eta-feature-builder`) that listens to `dispatch.load-events.v1` and the stop events from tracking-svc. It maintains per-load feature vectors in Redis under keys `etaf:{load_id}` with a 48-hour TTL. Features include remaining road distance, historical lane speed by hour of week, facility dwell percentiles, driver hours-of-service remaining, and weather severity along the route.
2. **eta-api** — a FastAPI app served by uvicorn on port 9400 with 4 workers per pod. It exposes `POST /v1/predict` (single) and `POST /v1/predict/batch` (up to 256 loads). Dispatch and the console call it through the gateway's internal route.
3. **eta-publisher** — a small scheduler that re-scores every in-flight load every 5 minutes and writes results to `eta.predictions.v1`.

## Model

Since April 2026 the production model is the temporal fusion transformer family, starting with `eta-tft-4.0.0` (ADR-024). The previous LightGBM model `eta-gbm-3.2.1` is kept in the MLflow registry in the Archived stage so it can be restored quickly. Models are loaded at pod start from the URI in `ETA_MODEL_URI`, which points at an MLflow model version (for example `models:/eta-predictor/Production`), with artifacts stored under `s3://nwf-ml-models/eta/`.

The transformer runs on CPU. We benchmarked GPU nodes and the latency gain did not justify the cost for batch sizes under 256. p95 latency budget for `/v1/predict` is 120 ms; the transformer sits around 70 ms, the old GBM at 15 ms.

The model outputs a point estimate plus a P10/P90 band. The console shows the band as the "ETA confidence band"; dispatch uses the P90 when deciding whether to warn a shipper of a late delivery.

## Fallback

If the model fails to load, the feature vector is missing, or inference exceeds 400 ms, eta-api returns a rules-based estimate: remaining distance divided by 50 mph, plus the facility's median dwell, plus a mandatory 30-minute break for every 8 hours of driving. Responses computed this way carry `"source": "fallback"` and the service logs error code ATL-5500. Fallback can also be forced for everyone with the Unleash flag `atlas.eta.force-fallback`, which is the first lever on-call pulls when predictions look wrong.

The environment variable `ETA_FALLBACK_MODE` controls behaviour when the model is missing at startup: `serve` (default, start and use rules) or `fail` (crash-loop, used in staging so that bad deploys are noticed).

## Training and promotion

Retraining runs weekly on Sunday at 02:00 UTC as an Argo Workflow (`eta-retrain`) owned by Jonah Pierce. It pulls the last 180 days of completed loads from the warehouse, trains, and registers a candidate version in MLflow at `mlflow.nwf.internal:5000`. Promotion to Production is manual and requires:

- MAE on the holdout week no worse than the current Production model by more than 3%.
- No segment (equipment type x region) regressing by more than 10%.
- A shadow period of 48 hours where the candidate scores live traffic but results are only logged.

The segment rule was added after INC-2026-019, when `eta-tft-4.0.0` looked fine in aggregate but was badly wrong for reefer loads in the Pacific Northwest because of a timezone feature bug. The fixed version was `eta-tft-4.0.3`.

## Observability

- Grafana "ML / ETA Model Drift" shows rolling MAE by segment, the share of fallback responses, and feature freshness.
- The metric `atlas_eta_fallback_total` with label `reason` (`model_unavailable`, `features_missing`, `timeout`, `forced`).
- PagerDuty service "Atlas ML" pages when fallback share exceeds 20% for 15 minutes or segment MAE exceeds 45 minutes.

## Dependencies and what breaks when

- Redis down: features missing, so everything falls back. ETAs degrade but nothing errors.
- Kafka lag on `dispatch.load-events.v1`: new loads have no features for a while, so they get fallback ETAs.
- MLflow down: only matters at pod start. Running pods keep their loaded model. This is why we never roll eta-api during an MLflow maintenance window.
- S3 access denied (this happened in INC-2025-014 when a security-group change blocked the VPC endpoint): pods cannot load the model and serve fallback.

## Code layout

- `ml/eta-predictor/app/` — FastAPI routes and schemas (pydantic v2).
- `ml/eta-predictor/features/` — shared feature definitions used by both the builder and training, so training/serving skew is limited to data freshness.
- `ml/eta-predictor/training/` — training code; notebooks are not allowed in this directory.
- `ml/eta-predictor/tests/` — pytest suite, including golden-file tests that pin predictions for 50 reference loads per model version.

## Scaling and resources

eta-api runs 6 replicas in production (HPA range 4–16) with 2 vCPU and 4 GiB of memory per pod; the transformer weights take about 900 MiB once loaded, and each uvicorn worker holds its own copy, which is why the worker count is 4 and not higher. The feature builder runs 3 replicas and is rarely the bottleneck. eta-publisher is a single replica with a Kubernetes Lease so that two copies never re-score the fleet at once; if it dies, the next scheduled run simply happens a few minutes late.

Batch scoring is the common path: eta-publisher sends `POST /v1/predict/batch` requests of 256 loads, and a full re-score of about 41,000 in-flight loads takes under two minutes.

When changing features, remember that the builder and the model must be deployed together; the feature schema version is stored in Redis alongside each vector (`schema_version`) and eta-api refuses vectors whose version does not match the loaded model's, falling back instead.

documents.title: atlas-gateway: edge routing and auth
documents.summary: The Go API gateway that terminates JWTs, rate-limits clients and fans REST calls out to gRPC services.
documents.body:
`atlas-gateway` is a thin Go service (chi router plus grpc-gateway generated handlers) listening on 8080. Responsibilities:

- Validate JWTs from Okta (console users) and from the partner-token service (API integrations).
- Per-client rate limiting: 600 req/min default, overrides in `gateway.ratelimit.overrides` in `config/atlas.yaml`. Limits are enforced with a Redis token bucket.
- Map REST paths under `/v1/` to internal gRPC calls.
- Stamp every request with `X-Atlas-Trace-Id`, which is echoed as `trace_id` in error responses.

It holds no business logic. If you find yourself adding a conditional based on load data in the gateway, it belongs in a service instead.

Routing tables are generated from the `google.api.http` annotations in `proto/`, so adding a REST endpoint means annotating the gRPC method rather than touching gateway code. The gateway also serves the OpenAPI spec at `/v1/openapi.json`, which the ops console uses to generate its client.

Timeouts: the gateway applies a 10-second overall request timeout and passes the remaining budget as the gRPC deadline. Uploads are the exception; they never pass through the gateway body, because docs-svc hands out presigned S3 URLs.

documents.title: dispatch-svc scope and dependencies
documents.summary: What dispatch-svc owns: loads, tenders, carrier assignment; synchronous deps on rate-engine and Postgres.
documents.body:
dispatch-svc owns the load lifecycle from creation to carrier assignment. Tables in the `dispatch` database: `loads`, `stops`, `tenders`, `load_assignments`, `carrier_capacity`, `outbox_events`.

Synchronous dependencies: Postgres (writer) and rate-engine over gRPC (50054). Everything else — notifications, ETA, billing — is downstream via `dispatch.load-events.v1`.

Capacity guard: a carrier may hold at most `DISPATCH_MAX_TENDERS_PER_CARRIER` open tenders (default 25). Offering one more is rejected with ATL-4012. A suspended carrier is rejected with ATL-4013 instead. The counter lives in `dispatch.carrier_capacity` and is updated in the same transaction as the tender row.

documents.title: rate-engine scope and pricing flow
documents.summary: What rate-engine does: lane pricing from contract and spot rates, cached quotes in Redis.
documents.body:
rate-engine answers one question: what should Northwind charge (and pay) for moving freight on a lane with a given equipment type on a given date. Its database is `rates`, with the main table `rates.lane_rates` (contract rates) and `rates.spot_observations` (market data ingested nightly from DAT).

Pricing order: customer contract rate if one exists, else spot median for the lane over 14 days with a margin from `rates.margin_rules`. If no lane matches the origin/destination 3-digit zip pair, it returns ATL-4221 (lane not found).

It is called synchronously by dispatch-svc when building a tender, so its latency is directly visible to users. Quotes are cached in Redis under `rq:{lane}:{equipment}`; see the rate-quote caching memories for TTLs.

Ports: HTTP 8084, gRPC 50054.

Margin rules are evaluated in priority order: shipper-specific rule, then lane-specific rule, then equipment default (dry van 14%, reefer 16%, flatbed 18%). A rule can set a floor and a ceiling in minor units, which is how the pricing team prevents spot volatility from producing absurd quotes on thin lanes.

The nightly DAT import runs at 04:30 UTC as the `rates-dat-import` CronJob and writes to `rates.spot_observations`; if it fails, quotes keep using the previous day's data and the metric `atlas_rates_spot_data_age_seconds` rises. Pricing questions go to Diego Salvatierra in #atlas-pricing.

documents.title: billing-svc: invoices and the ledger
documents.summary: How billing-svc turns delivered loads into invoices and records ledger postings.
documents.body:
billing-svc listens for `LoadDelivered` events and, once a POD reference from docs-svc is attached, drafts an invoice in `billing.invoices` with lines in `billing.invoice_lines`. Accessorials (detention, lumper, layover) are added from the stop records.

Every financial change is also appended to `billing.ledger_events` — the append-only ledger, never updated or deleted — and published to `billing.ledger.v1` via the outbox. The consumer group `billing-ledger-writer` projects ledger events into account balances in `billing.account_balances`.

Invoice finalisation takes a row lock on the invoice. If the lock cannot be obtained within `billing.invoice.lock_timeout_ms` (5000 ms), the request fails with ATL-5102 and is retried by the caller.

Money is always stored as `bigint` minor units plus a 3-letter ISO currency (ADR-026).

Two background jobs matter operationally:

- `billing-close` runs on the first business day of each month and locks the previous month's invoices for the finance close. It takes invoice row locks in batches of 500, which is the most common cause of ATL-5102 spikes.
- `carrier-settlement` runs daily at 06:00 UTC and creates carrier payables for delivered loads, honouring quick-pay requests.

Invoices are delivered to customers by email (PDF via SendGrid through notify-svc) or pushed to customer AP portals (Coupa, Ariba) by the `ap-portal-sync` worker.

documents.title: notify-svc delivery pipeline
documents.summary: How notify-svc consumes notification requests and delivers SMS, email and push.
documents.body:
Since the ADR-019 migration, notify-svc consumes `notify.requests.v1` (consumer group `notify-dispatcher`) instead of RabbitMQ. Any service can request a notification by writing an outbox row that becomes a message on that topic.

Channels and providers:
- SMS: Twilio primary, Sinch secondary (manual failover; see the SMS failover runbook).
- Email: SendGrid.
- Push: Firebase Cloud Messaging for the driver app.

Each request carries an `idempotency_key`; delivered keys are recorded in `notify.deliveries` for 7 days so retries do not double-text a driver. Templates live in `services/notify-svc/templates/` and are rendered with Go `text/template`. Quiet hours (21:00–06:00 in the driver's local timezone) apply to non-urgent SMS.

Port 8086. Failures that exhaust 5 retries go to `notify.requests.v1.dlq`.

Per-channel rate limits protect providers and recipients: at most 3 SMS per driver per 10 minutes (excess are coalesced into a single digest message), and outbound Twilio throughput is capped at 80 messages per second on the Atlas subaccount. The retry tiers (30 s, 2 min, 10 min) are separate topics, described in ADR-019.

Provider selection for SMS is controlled at runtime by the Unleash variant flag `atlas.notify.sms-provider`, so a Twilio outage can be handled without a deploy.

documents.title: docs-svc: BOL and POD storage
documents.summary: docs-svc stores bills of lading and proof-of-delivery files in S3 with metadata in Postgres.
documents.body:
docs-svc (port 8087) handles uploads of BOLs, PODs, lumper receipts and scale tickets. Files go to S3 bucket `nwf-atlas-docs-prod` under `{load_id}/{doc_type}/{uuid}`; metadata goes to `docs.documents`. Uploads use presigned PUT URLs valid for 15 minutes so large images never pass through the service.

After upload, an OCR job (AWS Textract) extracts signature presence and consignee name; if the POD lacks a signature, billing will not invoice automatically and a task appears in the console's exceptions queue.

documents.title: ops-console frontend structure
documents.summary: How the React ops console is built, routed and connected to the gateway.
documents.body:
The ops console (`web/ops-console`) is a React 18 single-page app built with Vite 5 and TypeScript 5, managed with pnpm 9 on Node 20. Key choices:

- **Routing**: React Router v6 with route modules under `src/routes/`.
- **Server state**: TanStack Query (ADR-021). Redux was removed in mid-2025; do not reintroduce global stores for server data.
- **UI kit**: internal `@nwf/atlas-ui` package built on Radix primitives, documented in Storybook.
- **Maps**: MapLibre GL with vector tiles from our own tile server.
- **Auth**: Okta OIDC with PKCE; tokens are kept in memory, refresh via hidden iframe.
- **API client**: generated from the gateway's OpenAPI spec with `openapi-typescript`; base URL comes from `VITE_ATLAS_API_BASE`.

The bundle is deployed to S3 and served via CloudFront; `index.html` is served with `Cache-Control: no-cache` after the May 2025 blank-screen incident, while hashed assets are immutable.

Feature areas map to route folders: `loads/` (the dispatch board), `tracking/` (live map), `billing/` (invoice review and exceptions), `carriers/` (onboarding, scorecards) and `admin/`. Each area owns its own query keys, defined in a `queries.ts` file next to the routes, so cache invalidation after a mutation is local and explicit.

The live map subscribes to the tracking SSE stream through a small hook, `useTrackStream(loadId)`, which reconnects with exponential backoff capped at 30 seconds. End-to-end tests run in Playwright against the staging gateway on every merge to `main`.

documents.title: Transactional outbox and the outbox-relay process
documents.summary: How services publish Kafka events reliably through outbox tables and the outbox-relay.
documents.body:
Every service that emits events has an `outbox_events` table in its own database with columns `id bigserial`, `topic`, `key`, `payload bytea`, `headers jsonb`, `created_at`, `published_at`.

Application code inserts outbox rows in the same transaction as the business change. `outbox-relay` (one deployment per database, 2 replicas with leader election via a Postgres advisory lock) polls every 250 ms, selecting up to 500 unpublished rows `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, publishes them to Kafka with idempotent producer settings, and marks them published. Published rows are deleted after 3 days by a cleanup job.

Because the leader lock is session-level, outbox-relay connects to the Aurora writer directly on 5432 and does not go through PgBouncer. This is the one exception to the "always use PgBouncer" rule.

Ordering guarantee: per key, in commit order. Consumers must still be idempotent because a relay crash between publish and mark can produce a duplicate.

Operational notes:
- The metric `atlas_outbox_unpublished_rows` per database is the best early warning. Anything above 5,000 for more than two minutes usually means the relay lost its leader lock or Kafka is rejecting produces.
- If the relay is stuck, `atlasctl outbox status --db dispatch` shows the current leader pod, the oldest unpublished row and the last produce error.
- Never delete rows from `outbox_events` by hand to "unstick" things; that silently drops events that downstream services (billing in particular) depend on.

documents.title: Rate-quote cache TTL is 15 minutes
documents.summary: rate-engine caches lane quotes in Redis for 900 seconds.
documents.body: rate-engine caches computed quotes in Redis at `rq:{lane}:{equipment}` with a fixed TTL of 900 seconds (15 minutes), set by `rates.cache.quote_ttl_seconds`. Spot data only changes nightly, so 15 minutes was considered safe. Cache misses recompute from Postgres, which takes 40–120 ms.

documents.title: Rate-quote cache TTL reduced to 5 minutes with jitter
documents.summary: After INC-2025-047, quote TTL is 300s plus up to 60s random jitter; supersedes the 15-minute TTL.
documents.body:
Supersedes `rate-quote-cache-ttl-15m`.

Following the Redis eviction incident INC-2025-047, rate-engine now caches quotes for 300 seconds plus a random jitter of 0–60 seconds (`rates.cache.quote_ttl_seconds: 300`, `rates.cache.quote_ttl_jitter_seconds: 60`). The shorter TTL cut the working set in Redis by about 60%, and the jitter prevents thousands of hot lanes from expiring in the same second and stampeding Postgres.

Cache fills are also now protected with a singleflight per key inside each pod, so a miss on a hot lane triggers one recomputation per pod rather than one per request.

documents.title: What Redis is and is not used for
documents.summary: Redis in Atlas is limited to rate-quote cache, ETA features, dedupe sets, rate limiting and sessions.
documents.body:
Allowed uses of the ElastiCache cluster, with key prefixes:

- `rq:` — rate-engine quote cache
- `etaf:` — ETA feature vectors (48h TTL)
- `dd:` — tracking ping dedupe sets (10 min TTL)
- `rl:` — gateway rate-limit buckets
- `sess:` — ops-console server-side session metadata

Anything else needs a platform review. Every key must have a TTL; the `atlas-redis-lint` CI check greps for `SET` calls without an expiry in Go code. Redis is never the source of truth — a full flush must be survivable with only a latency hit.

documents.title: Aurora Postgres topology and connection paths
documents.summary: One Aurora PostgreSQL 15 cluster with one database per service, accessed through PgBouncer.
documents.body:
Production runs a single Aurora PostgreSQL 15.6 cluster `atlas-prod` with one writer (db.r6g.2xlarge) and two readers. Databases: `dispatch`, `tracking`, `billing`, `rates`, `notify`, `docs`. Each service has its own login role and cannot see other databases.

Application pods connect through PgBouncer (transaction pooling) rather than directly. Read-only endpoints like the console's reporting pages use the reader endpoint through a second PgBouncer pool. Long-running analytics must go to the warehouse, not the readers.

An Aurora Global Database secondary runs in us-west-2 for DR with typical replication lag under one second.

Exact host names and ports are recorded in the environment memories.

Instance roles today: the writer handles all service writes plus outbox polling; reader 1 serves the console's reporting pages and `atlasctl db psql` read-only sessions; reader 2 is reserved for the warehouse CDC export and is excluded from the reader endpoint via a custom endpoint `atlas-prod-analytics`. Storage is Aurora I/O-Optimized. The largest database by far is `tracking` (roughly 2 TB with 90 days of pings), followed by `billing` (about 400 GB including detached archive partitions).

documents.title: Kafka topic catalog
documents.summary: List of Atlas Kafka topics with partitions, retention, keys, producers and consumers.
documents.body:
| Topic | Partitions | Retention | Key | Producer | Main consumers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dispatch.load-events.v1` | 24 | 7d | `load_id` | dispatch-svc (outbox) | tracking-ingest, eta-feature-builder, billing, console-sse |
| `telemetry.gps.v2` | 48 | 72h | `truck_id` | tracking webhooks, driver app | tracking-ingest |
| `billing.ledger.v1` | 12 | 30d | `account_id` | billing-svc (outbox) | billing-ledger-writer, warehouse-sink |
| `notify.requests.v1` | 12 | 3d | `recipient_id` | any service | notify-dispatcher |
| `eta.predictions.v1` | 24 | 24h | `load_id` | eta-publisher | dispatch-svc, console-sse |
| `edi.inbound.v1` | 6 | 14d | `carrier_scac` | edi-bridge | dispatch-svc |

Every topic has a matching `.dlq` topic with 14-day retention. Topic creation goes through the `kafka_topics` Terraform module in atlas-infra; auto-create is disabled on the brokers.

People frequently assume `billing.ledger.v1` is log-compacted. It is not; it uses normal delete retention, and the warehouse sink is the long-term copy.

documents.title: Authentication and service-to-service identity
documents.summary: Humans authenticate with Okta OIDC, partners with scoped JWTs, services with Linkerd mTLS.
documents.body:
- **Humans (ops console)**: Okta OIDC with PKCE. Group claims map to Atlas roles: `atlas-dispatcher`, `atlas-billing`, `atlas-admin`, `atlas-readonly`.
- **Partners / integrations**: the partner-token service issues short-lived (1 hour) JWTs from client credentials; scopes like `loads:write`, `tracking:read`. Client secrets are stored hashed in `gateway.partner_clients`.
- **Service to service**: Linkerd mTLS provides identity; services authorize callers using the Linkerd `l5d-client-id` header against an allowlist in each service's config. No shared API keys between services.

The gateway is the only component that validates end-user JWTs; it forwards the subject and roles to services in `x-atlas-subject` and `x-atlas-roles` metadata.

Role mapping lives in `services/atlas-gateway/config/roles.yaml`. `atlas-admin` is granted to about ten people and audited quarterly by Grace Okafor. Partner client credentials are created with `atlasctl partners create-client --name "<partner>" --scopes loads:write,tracking:read`, which prints the secret once; it's never retrievable again, only rotatable. Okta group membership changes take effect at the user's next token refresh, which is at most one hour later; forcing a logout from the console's profile menu applies them immediately.

documents.title: Observability stack: metrics, logs, traces
documents.summary: Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and Grafana with OpenTelemetry instrumentation across Atlas.
documents.body:
Following ADR-018, all services are instrumented with OpenTelemetry SDKs and export OTLP to the collector at `otel-collector.observability:4317`. The collector fans out:

- metrics → Prometheus (also scraped directly from `:9090/metrics`), 30-day retention, long-term in Thanos
- traces → Tempo, 14-day retention, 10% head sampling plus 100% of error traces
- logs → Loki via promtail, 30 days

Grafana is at `https://grafana.nwf.internal`. Trace IDs appear in logs as `trace_id` so you can jump from a Loki line to Tempo. Alerts are defined as code in `atlas-infra/monitoring/alerts/` and route to PagerDuty.

documents.title: DR topology: warm standby in us-west-2
documents.summary: Atlas runs a warm standby in us-west-2 with Aurora Global Database and MSK replication; RTO 60 min, RPO 5 min.
documents.body:
Per ADR-023, us-west-2 hosts:

- Aurora Global Database secondary cluster `atlas-dr` (promotable in about 1 minute).
- MSK cluster `atlas-dr-msk` fed by MirrorMaker 2 for all topics except `telemetry.gps.v2` (pings are considered re-sendable and too expensive to mirror).
- EKS cluster `atlas-dr-eks` with all Argo CD apps synced but scaled to 0 replicas.
- S3 cross-region replication for `nwf-atlas-docs-prod`.

A regional failover is a human decision by the incident commander plus the CTO. Game days run twice a year; the last one (2026-03) achieved full service in 47 minutes.

documents.title: Tender state machine
documents.summary: Valid tender states and transitions in dispatch-svc, including expiry and cancellation rules.
documents.body:
Tender states in `dispatch.tenders.status`:

`DRAFT` → `OFFERED` → one of `ACCEPTED`, `REJECTED`, `EXPIRED`, `WITHDRAWN`.

Rules:
- Only `OFFERED` tenders count toward a carrier's open-tender capacity (ATL-4012 limit).
- `OFFERED` becomes `EXPIRED` after `dispatch.tender.expiry_seconds` (600 s) via the `tender-expirer` loop, which runs every 15 seconds.
- `ACCEPTED` is terminal for the tender but creates a `load_assignments` row; un-assigning later is a new `ASSIGNMENT_REVOKED` load event, not a tender transition.
- A load can have many tenders but at most one `ACCEPTED`. Accepting a second one returns ATL-4090 (conflict).

Transitions are enforced in `services/dispatch-svc/internal/tender/fsm.go`; the table also has a check constraint, so a bad transition fails at the database even if code is wrong.

Every transition emits a load event (`TenderOffered`, `TenderAccepted`, `TenderRejected`, `TenderExpired`, `TenderWithdrawn`) through the outbox, with the previous and new status in the payload. Downstream consumers should key off the event type rather than diffing statuses. Rejection reasons from carriers are normalised into `dispatch.tender_reject_reasons` (for example `NO_CAPACITY`, `RATE_TOO_LOW`, `EQUIPMENT_MISMATCH`), which feed the carrier scorecard.

documents.title: How idempotency keys work on write APIs
documents.summary: Write endpoints accept Idempotency-Key headers stored for 24 hours; mismatched replays return ATL-4090.
documents.body:
Per ADR-022, `POST` and `PATCH` endpoints on loads and tenders accept an `Idempotency-Key` header (UUID recommended). dispatch-svc stores `(client_id, key)` with a SHA-256 hash of the request body and the response in `dispatch.idempotency_keys` for 24 hours.

- Same key, same body: the stored response is replayed with header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`.
- Same key, different body: 409 with error ATL-4090.
- Concurrent requests with the same key: the second waits on a row lock up to 2 s, then returns 409.

EDI-originated tenders use the EDI interchange control number as the key, so duplicate 204s from carriers are harmless.

Keys are scoped per client: two different partners may use the same UUID without colliding. Expired keys are purged hourly by the `idempotency-janitor` loop. The console generates a fresh key per user action (a click on "Offer tender"), not per HTTP attempt, so its automatic retries are safe. If you see ATL-4090 in console logs, it almost always means a double-submit bug where the same key was reused for a modified form.

documents.title: edi-bridge: EDI 204/990/214 integration
documents.summary: edi-bridge translates carrier EDI transactions over AS2/SFTP into Atlas API calls and events.
documents.body:
Large carriers still integrate via EDI. `edi-bridge` handles:

- **204** (load tender) outbound to carriers when dispatch offers a tender.
- **990** (tender response) inbound → accept/reject calls to dispatch.
- **214** (shipment status) inbound → converted to low-resolution pings and stop events.

Transport is AS2 for the top 12 carriers and SFTP polling (every 5 min) for the rest. Parsed messages are published to `edi.inbound.v1` keyed by carrier SCAC. Raw EDI files are archived to `s3://nwf-atlas-edi-archive/` for 7 years for audit.

Partner-specific quirks (segment terminators, custom N9 qualifiers) are configured per SCAC in `services/edi-bridge/partners/*.yaml`.

documents.title: ADR-001: Go for all backend services
documents.summary: Atlas backend services are written in Go; Python is allowed only for ML workloads.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted (2025-01-08). **Deciders:** Rosalind Achebe, Priya Raman, Tomasz Wierzbicki.

We standardise on Go (currently 1.23) for every backend service. Reasons: small static binaries, predictable latency, good gRPC and Kafka libraries, and most of the team already writes it. Python is permitted only under `ml/` for model training and serving (eta-predictor). New languages require a new ADR.

documents.title: ADR-003: Postgres as system of record, one database per service
documents.summary: Each Atlas service owns its own Postgres database on the shared Aurora cluster and never reads another's tables.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted.

Every service gets its own logical database and login role on the Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Cross-service reads happen through APIs or events, never SQL joins across databases. We accept some data duplication (for example, billing keeps a copy of stop addresses) in exchange for independent schema evolution.

Consequences: reporting across domains happens in the warehouse (Snowflake via the Kafka sink), not in production Postgres. The data platform team maintains dbt models that join domain events into analytics tables; if a dashboard needs data from two services, it is built there.

Enforcement is mechanical: each service's login role (`dispatch_app`, `tracking_app`, `billing_app`, `rates_app`, `notify_app`, `docs_app`) has `CONNECT` only on its own database, and a CI check rejects SQL files that reference another service's schema name. A single cluster keeps costs down; if one service's load becomes disruptive we will split it onto its own cluster, starting with `tracking`, which is by far the largest.

documents.title: ADR-005: Kafka on Amazon MSK as the event backbone
documents.summary: Atlas uses Amazon MSK (Kafka 3.6) for all domain events and telemetry, provisioned via Terraform.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted.

We chose managed Kafka (MSK, Kafka 3.6, 6 brokers of kafka.m7g.xlarge across 3 AZs) over Kinesis and self-hosted Kafka. Kinesis shard limits made the GPS firehose awkward, and self-hosting was not worth the operational load for a team our size. Authentication is SASL/SCRAM with per-service users; ACLs are managed in Terraform.

At the time notify-svc was explicitly excluded and kept on RabbitMQ (ADR-007) because it needed per-message delayed retries. That exclusion was later reversed by ADR-019.

Broker settings that differ from MSK defaults: `auto.create.topics.enable=false`, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `default.replication.factor=3`, and `log.retention.hours=168` as a default that topics normally override. Tomasz Wierzbicki owns the cluster in Terraform; day-to-day operations such as lag alerting and consumer tuning sit with Samir Haddad.

documents.title: ADR-007: RabbitMQ (Amazon MQ) for notify-svc
documents.summary: notify-svc will consume notification requests from RabbitMQ on Amazon MQ to get delayed retries.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted (2025-02-18). Owner: Aiko Tanabe.

notify-svc needs per-message delayed retries (for example, retry an SMS after 30 s, then 2 min, then 10 min) and quiet-hours deferral. RabbitMQ's delayed-message exchange gives us this out of the box, while Kafka would require retry topics. We will run RabbitMQ 3.12 on Amazon MQ (`mq.m5.large`, single-instance in staging, active/standby in prod) with the exchange `notify.requests` and queue `notify-dispatcher`.

Services publish notification requests through their outbox; outbox-relay gets a RabbitMQ publisher for this one destination.

Alternatives considered: Kafka with retry topics (rejected as extra work for the notification team at the time), and SQS (rejected because it would be yet another messaging system). Monitoring for the broker lives in a dedicated "Notify / RabbitMQ" Grafana dashboard, and the queue depth alert pages the notify owner.

documents.title: ADR-009: Transactional outbox for event publishing
documents.summary: Services write events to an outbox table in the same transaction; outbox-relay publishes them to Kafka.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted.

Dual writes (commit to Postgres, then publish to Kafka) lose events when a pod dies between the two. We adopt the transactional outbox: business change and event row commit together, and a relay publishes asynchronously. We rejected Debezium CDC because it would add Kafka Connect to operate and couples events to table schemas.

Trade-offs accepted: a few hundred milliseconds of extra latency, and consumers must tolerate duplicates.

documents.title: ADR-011: gRPC between services, REST at the edge
documents.summary: Internal service calls use gRPC with protobufs in proto/; external clients use REST/JSON via atlas-gateway.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted.

Internal synchronous calls use gRPC with contracts in `proto/` (managed by buf, breaking-change detection in CI). External clients — the ops console, shipper portals and partner integrations — get REST/JSON through atlas-gateway, generated with grpc-gateway so the two surfaces cannot drift. Deadlines are mandatory on every internal call; the default is 2 seconds and dispatch → rate-engine uses 800 ms.

documents.title: ADR-012: Daily partitioning for tracking.gps_pings
documents.summary: tracking.gps_pings is range-partitioned by day with pg_partman and retained for 90 days.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Marcus Oyelaran.

The ping table grows by about 22 GB/day. We partition `tracking.gps_pings` by day on `recorded_at` using pg_partman 5, pre-creating 7 days ahead. Partitions older than 90 days are dropped (not detached-and-archived) because raw pings are also exported to S3 Parquet by the warehouse sink.

Daily granularity keeps each partition around 22 GB, which makes index builds and drops fast. Hourly was considered and rejected: too many relations for the planner.

Maintenance is done by the shared `partman-maintenance` CronJob in the `atlas` namespace, hourly. An alert fires when fewer than 3 future partitions exist, added after INC-2026-015, when the CronJob failed silently for eight days and pings fell into the default partition. Queries must always bound `recorded_at`; the `partition-guard` CI check enforces this for code in tracking-svc.

documents.title: ADR-013: Monthly partitioning for billing.ledger_events
documents.summary: billing.ledger_events is range-partitioned by month and retained for 7 years for audit.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Hannah Kowalczyk (at the time).

The ledger is append-only and must be retained for 7 years for tax audits. We partition `billing.ledger_events` by month on `posted_at` with pg_partman, pre-creating 3 months ahead. Partitions older than 13 months are detached and moved to the `billing_archive` schema on cheaper storage (Aurora I/O-Optimized is not needed for them), but never dropped before 7 years.

Monthly granularity fits the finance close process, which queries one month at a time. Unlike the tracking ping table, dropping partitions is forbidden here; the retention job for billing only detaches.

Implementation details:
- The partman config lives in `billing.part_config` and is maintained by the `billing-partman` CronJob on the 1st of each month at 03:00 UTC, not by the shared `partman-maintenance` job used for tracking.
- Queries from billing-svc must include `posted_at` bounds. The invoice detail page queries at most the invoice month plus one month either side.
- Restoring an archived partition for an audit means re-attaching it with `ALTER TABLE ... ATTACH PARTITION`; Yusuf Demir has a script for this in `services/billing-svc/scripts/reattach_partition.sql`.

documents.title: ADR-014: LightGBM gradient-boosted model for ETA
documents.summary: ETA predictions use a LightGBM model (eta-gbm v3) served from FastAPI with a rules-based fallback.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted (2025-03-05). Owner: Farah Nadeem.

We will serve ETAs from a LightGBM regression model, `eta-gbm` v3 (currently `eta-gbm-3.2.1`), trained on 180 days of completed loads. Features are tabular: remaining distance, lane historical speed, facility dwell, hours-of-service, weather. The model is small (~40 MB), scores in ~15 ms on CPU and is easy to explain to operations using SHAP values.

Deep-learning sequence models were considered but deferred until we have better feature pipelines for GPS sequences. Holdout MAE for v3.2.1 is 17.4 minutes.

Consequences: eta-api pods are small (1 GiB memory, 4 replicas). Retraining is weekly on CPU nodes and takes about 40 minutes. The model's features are all tabular, so feature engineering happens in the eta-feature-builder and in SQL for training. A rules-based fallback is kept for when the model is unavailable; responses from it log ATL-5500. Model artifacts are registered in MLflow under the name `eta-predictor`. Until a dedicated ML engineer is hired, Farah Nadeem runs the weekly retraining job by hand and reviews each run herself.

documents.title: ADR-015: Argo CD and Argo Rollouts for deployments
documents.summary: Deployments move from the Jenkins atlas-deploy job to GitOps with Argo CD and canary rollouts.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Tomasz Wierzbicki.

The Jenkins `atlas-deploy` job gave us no drift detection and rollbacks meant re-running a job with an older version. We move to Argo CD with an app-of-apps (`atlas-apps`) reading manifests from `deploy/` in the monorepo, and Argo Rollouts for canaries (10% → 30% → 60% → 100% with Prometheus analysis between steps).

Image tags are bumped by CI committing to `deploy/envs/<env>/<svc>/values.yaml`. Jenkins is decommissioned for deploys at the end of June 2025.

Alternatives considered: Flux (similar, but the team already knew Argo from a previous employer) and Spinnaker (too heavy). The canary analysis template `atlas-default-canary` checks HTTP 5xx ratio below 1% and p99 latency within 20% of the stable version over 5 minutes at each step; a failing check aborts and scales the canary to zero automatically. Services can override thresholds in their own `AnalysisTemplate`. Production syncs are manual (someone clicks sync or runs `argocd app sync`), while staging auto-syncs on every merge.

documents.title: ADR-016: AWS Secrets Manager with External Secrets Operator
documents.summary: Application secrets move from SSM Parameter Store to AWS Secrets Manager synced by External Secrets Operator.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Grace Okafor.

SSM Parameter Store SecureStrings had no native rotation and every service fetched them at startup with its own code. We adopt AWS Secrets Manager with one JSON secret per service per environment (`atlas/<env>/<svc>`) and the External Secrets Operator syncing them into Kubernetes Secrets every hour. Rotation Lambdas are enabled for Postgres credentials (every 30 days). Migration target: end of August 2025.

documents.title: ADR-017: One monorepo for application code
documents.summary: All Atlas application code (Go, TypeScript, Python) lives in northwind/atlas; infrastructure stays separate.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted.

Services, the ops console, the ML service, protobufs and atlasctl live in `github.com/northwind/atlas`. We use a Go workspace (`go.work`) and pnpm workspaces rather than Bazel; CI uses path filters so a change to `services/billing-svc/**` only builds billing. Terraform stays in `northwind/atlas-infra` so that infra permissions (Atlantis) can be scoped separately.

documents.title: ADR-018: OpenTelemetry for metrics, traces and logs correlation
documents.summary: All services instrument with OpenTelemetry and export OTLP to a central collector.
documents.body: **Status:** Accepted. We replace ad-hoc Prometheus client usage and the Jaeger agent with OpenTelemetry SDKs everywhere (Go, Python, browser). Services export OTLP gRPC to `otel-collector.observability:4317`. Trace context propagates through Kafka message headers (`traceparent`) so an ops-console click can be followed through dispatch, outbox-relay, and downstream consumers.

documents.title: ADR-019: Move notify-svc from RabbitMQ to Kafka
documents.summary: notify-svc will consume notify.requests.v1 from Kafka with retry topics, retiring Amazon MQ; supersedes ADR-007.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted (2025-11-03). **Supersedes:** `adr-007-rabbitmq-for-notifications`. **Owner:** Aiko Tanabe. **Reviewers:** Samir Haddad, Tomasz Wierzbicki, Priya Raman.

## Context

ADR-007 put notify-svc on RabbitMQ (Amazon MQ) because we wanted per-message delayed retries without building them ourselves. Nine months later, that decision has cost more than it saved:

- **Two messaging systems.** Every on-call engineer needs to understand both Kafka and RabbitMQ. The RabbitMQ runbooks were thin and only Aiko really knew the broker. During INC-2025-044 (the SMS rate-limit incident on 2025-10-06 was the final straw, but there were three earlier near misses) the queue depth graph lived in a different Grafana folder than everything else and nobody on call found it for twenty minutes.
- **Outbox-relay special-casing.** The relay has a RabbitMQ publisher used by exactly one destination. It has its own reconnect logic, its own bugs (ATLAS-1590, publisher confirms silently disabled after reconnect) and its own tests.
- **No replay.** When a template bug sent wrong pickup times to about 1,100 drivers in September, we could not replay the corrected notifications from the broker because RabbitMQ had already acked and deleted them. With Kafka we could have reset the consumer group offset.
- **Cost.** The active/standby `mq.m5.large` pair costs more per month than the extra partitions we need on MSK, which already has headroom.
- **Delayed retries turned out to be simple.** The only retry schedules we actually use are 30 s, 2 min and 10 min. Those map cleanly to three retry topics.

## Decision

notify-svc moves to Kafka.

- Requests are published to `notify.requests.v1` (12 partitions, 3-day retention, keyed by `recipient_id` so one driver's notifications stay ordered).
- The consumer group is `notify-dispatcher`.
- Retries use tiered retry topics: `notify.requests.retry.30s`, `notify.requests.retry.2m`, `notify.requests.retry.10m`. A small retry consumer inside notify-svc reads each retry topic, sleeps until the message's `not_before` header, and re-publishes to the main topic. After the 10-minute tier, messages go to `notify.requests.v1.dlq`.
- Quiet hours are implemented by setting `not_before` to the end of the quiet window and routing to the 10-minute retry tier repeatedly until it is due. This is less elegant than the RabbitMQ delayed exchange but has proven fine in load tests up to 5,000 deferred messages.
- Idempotency: each request has an `idempotency_key`, and delivered keys are kept in `notify.deliveries` for 7 days. This existed already and is what makes Kafka redelivery safe.
- outbox-relay loses its RabbitMQ publisher entirely.

### Message format

The message schema is `atlas.notify.v1.NotificationRequest` in `proto/atlas/notify/v1/request.proto`. Fields that matter operationally:

- `channel` (`SMS`, `EMAIL`, `PUSH`), `template_id`, and `template_vars` (a string map).
- `recipient_id` plus a resolved `recipient_address` snapshot, so a phone-number change mid-flight does not redirect an in-flight message.
- `urgency` (`ROUTINE` or `URGENT`). Only `URGENT` bypasses quiet hours; today that is used for pickup-cancelled and hazmat-related notices only.
- Kafka headers `not_before` (RFC 3339 timestamp), `attempt` (integer, starting at 1) and the usual `traceparent`.

The retry consumer increments `attempt` each time it re-publishes. Anything reaching the DLQ carries the last provider error in the header `last_error` (for example `twilio:21610` for an opted-out number), which is what on-call reads first when triaging the DLQ.

### Capacity

Normal volume is about 180 notifications per minute, peaking near 2,500 per minute during the 06:00–08:00 Eastern dispatch rush. Twelve partitions with 3 notify-svc replicas handle ten times that in load tests, so partition count is not expected to change for years.

## Alternatives considered

1. **Keep RabbitMQ, invest in runbooks.** Rejected: doesn't fix replay or the dual-system cognitive load.
2. **Amazon SQS with delay queues.** Rejected: delay is capped at 15 minutes (fine) but it would be a third messaging technology, and SQS doesn't give us ordered per-recipient processing without FIFO queues and their throughput limits.
3. **Kafka with a scheduler service** (a generic delayed-delivery service backed by Postgres). Rejected as over-engineering for three fixed retry intervals.

## Migration plan

1. Create topics via the `kafka_topics` Terraform module (ticket ATLAS-2011). Tomasz reviews the Terraform; Samir sets up lag alerts for `notify-dispatcher` in the same "Atlas / Kafka Consumer Lag" dashboard as everything else.
2. Dual-publish from outbox-relay for one week: every notification request goes to both RabbitMQ and Kafka, while notify-svc continues to consume only from RabbitMQ. Compare counts daily.
3. Flip the Unleash flag `atlas.notify.consume-from-kafka` in staging, then in prod during a low-traffic window (Sunday morning Eastern).
4. Keep RabbitMQ running but idle for two weeks as a rollback path.
5. Decommission Amazon MQ and remove the RabbitMQ publisher from outbox-relay (ATLAS-2034).

Target completion: 2025-12-15. The peak-season change freeze (November 24 to December 2) means step 3 happens either before or after it, not during.

## Consequences

- One messaging system for on-call to learn. The RabbitMQ runbooks will be archived; the Kafka consumer-lag runbooks become the reference for notify issues too.
- Replay is available via `atlasctl kafka reset-offsets --group notify-dispatcher --to-datetime ...`, but replaying notifications is dangerous (it texts drivers). The runbook requires approval from the notify owner before any offset reset on this group.
- Latency for retries is slightly coarser (a message due in 30 s may be delivered at 31–35 s). Product (Mei-Ling Zhou) confirmed that is acceptable.
- The notify-svc Grafana panels move into the standard "Atlas / Kafka Consumer Lag" dashboard. The old "Notify / RabbitMQ" dashboard will be deleted after decommissioning.

## Follow-up (added 2025-12-18)

Migration completed on 2025-12-11. Amazon MQ broker `atlas-notify-mq` was deleted on 2025-12-17. Final dual-publish comparison showed zero missing messages and 14 duplicates, all absorbed by the idempotency check. The retry-tier design has since been reused by the edi-bridge for outbound 204 retries.

documents.title: ADR-020: Self-hosted Unleash for feature flags
documents.summary: Feature flags are served by a self-hosted Unleash instance; flag names follow atlas.<service>.<flag>.
documents.body: **Status:** Accepted. We replaced config-file toggles with self-hosted Unleash 5 at `https://flags.nwf.internal`, backed by its own small RDS instance. Go services use the official Go SDK with a 15-second refresh; the console uses the frontend proxy. LaunchDarkly was evaluated but rejected on cost. Every flag must have an owner and an expiry date in its description; stale flags are reported weekly in #atlas-platform.

documents.title: ADR-021: TanStack Query instead of Redux for server state
documents.summary: The ops console manages server state with TanStack Query; Redux Toolkit is removed.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Lena Brandt.

About 80% of the Redux store in the ops console was cached API responses with hand-written loading flags and invalidation. We replace it with TanStack Query v5, using query keys defined per feature area. Remaining client-only state (panel layout, map filters) uses component state or small Zustand stores. Migration was done feature by feature and finished in July 2025; the `redux` and `@reduxjs/toolkit` packages are banned by an ESLint rule.

documents.title: ADR-022: Idempotency keys on write APIs
documents.summary: Load and tender write endpoints require clients to send Idempotency-Key headers, stored for 24 hours.
documents.body: **Status:** Accepted. Carriers' integrations retry aggressively on timeouts, and in Q1 2025 we saw 312 duplicate tenders in one week. We adopt Stripe-style idempotency keys for `POST`/`PATCH` on loads and tenders, stored 24 hours. Partner API clients must send them (enforced from 2025-07-01, requests without one get HTTP 400); the console sends them automatically. Conflicting reuse returns ATL-4090.

documents.title: ADR-023: Warm-standby disaster recovery in us-west-2
documents.summary: Atlas DR is a warm standby in us-west-2 with RTO 60 minutes and RPO 5 minutes.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Deciders: Rosalind Achebe, Tomasz Wierzbicki, Samir Haddad.

Options were backup-and-restore (RTO ~8 h), warm standby, or active-active. Active-active was rejected because dispatch's tender logic assumes a single writer. Warm standby keeps data replicated continuously (Aurora Global Database, MirrorMaker 2, S3 CRR) and compute defined but scaled to zero, giving an RTO of 60 minutes and RPO of 5 minutes at roughly 18% of prod infrastructure cost. GPS telemetry is not mirrored.

documents.title: ADR-024: Temporal fusion transformer (eta-tft v4) replaces LightGBM
documents.summary: ETA serving moves from eta-gbm v3 to the eta-tft v4 transformer model; supersedes ADR-014.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted (2026-04-02). **Supersedes:** `adr-014-eta-lightgbm-model`. **Owner:** Farah Nadeem. **Contributors:** Jonah Pierce, Marcus Oyelaran (feature pipeline), Priya Raman (dispatch integration).

## Context

ADR-014 chose a LightGBM regressor for ETA prediction in March 2025, explicitly deferring sequence models "until we have better feature pipelines for GPS sequences." Those pipelines now exist: since the tracking-svc improvements in late 2025, `tracking.load_track_segments` gives clean per-load movement segments, and the eta-feature-builder can maintain a rolling window of the last 12 segments for every in-flight load.

Meanwhile, `eta-gbm-3.2.1` has plateaued. Holdout MAE has hovered around 17 minutes for a year, and retraining no longer moves it. Its errors are concentrated in exactly the situations operations cares most about:

- multi-stop LTL routes, where the model treats each leg independently;
- loads that are already running late, where recent movement is the best predictor but the GBM only sees a single "average speed so far" feature;
- long-haul reefer loads with mandated breaks.

Shippers complain about ETAs that stay optimistic until the last hour and then jump. Customer success estimates that ETA accuracy is mentioned in about a third of escalations.

## Decision

Replace `eta-gbm` with a temporal fusion transformer model family named `eta-tft`, starting with version `eta-tft-4.0.0`. The model consumes:

- static covariates: equipment type, lane, carrier, shipper, facility IDs (embedded);
- known future inputs: scheduled appointment windows, hours-of-service remaining, forecast weather along the route, time-of-week;
- observed history: the last 12 movement segments from tracking (speed, stop duration, deviation from planned route).

It outputs quantiles P10, P50 and P90. P50 is the displayed ETA; P10–P90 becomes the console's confidence band; dispatch uses P90 for late-delivery warnings. The GBM produced only a point estimate, so the band is new for users.

Serving stays in `eta-api` (FastAPI on port 9400) on CPU. We measured:

| Model | Holdout MAE | p95 latency (single) | Artifact size |
|---|---|---|---|
| eta-gbm-3.2.1 | 17.4 min | 15 ms | 40 MB |
| eta-tft-4.0.0 | 11.2 min | 70 ms | 880 MB |

The 120 ms p95 budget still holds. Pods need 4 GiB memory instead of 1 GiB, and each uvicorn worker loads its own copy of the weights, so we reduce workers to 4 per pod and increase replicas from 4 to 6.

## What does not change

- The API contract of `/v1/predict` and `/v1/predict/batch` is unchanged apart from new optional fields `p10_minutes` and `p90_minutes`.
- The rules-based fallback and error code ATL-5500 remain. The flag `atlas.eta.force-fallback` still works.
- `ETA_MODEL_URI` still points at an MLflow model reference; only the registered model version changes.
- Weekly retraining stays on Sunday 02:00 UTC, but training moves to a GPU node pool (`ml-train-g5`) because transformer training on CPU takes 19 hours.

## Rollout

1. Shadow mode for two weeks: `eta-tft-4.0.0` scores all traffic in parallel and results are logged to `eta.shadow_predictions` but not served.
2. Canary by region: Southeast first (lowest volume), then Midwest, then everyone. Controlled by the Unleash flag `atlas.eta.model-v4-regions`.
3. Keep `eta-gbm-3.2.1` loadable in the MLflow registry (stage Archived) for at least 90 days so rollback is a config change plus a rollout restart, not a retrain. The rollback procedure is in the ETA model rollback runbook.

## Evaluation methodology

Offline evaluation used the 8 most recent complete weeks as holdout, with a strict time split (no load in holdout had any leg in the training window). We report MAE on minutes of error at three horizons: at dispatch (typically 12–48 hours before delivery), at pickup departure, and at 2 hours before the appointment. The transformer's gain is largest at the pickup-departure horizon (21.9 → 12.8 minutes) and smallest at the 2-hour horizon (6.1 → 5.4 minutes), which matches intuition: late in the trip, simple extrapolation is already good.

Segments were defined as equipment type (dry van, reefer, flatbed) crossed with the six operating regions (Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, South Central, Mountain, Pacific Northwest/West). At the time of this ADR all eighteen segments improved offline, the smallest gain being flatbed in Mountain (−4%). The offline set, however, did not include the week of the US daylight-saving change, which later turned out to matter.

## Operational ownership

- Farah Nadeem owns the model and the promotion decision.
- Jonah Pierce owns the `eta-retrain` workflow and the GPU node pool budget.
- Marcus Oyelaran owns the segment features coming from tracking.
- Pages from PagerDuty service "Atlas ML" go to the ML on-call rotation during business hours and to the Atlas Core primary out of hours, who is expected to force the fallback flag rather than debug the model.

## Risks

- **Aggregate metrics can hide segment regressions.** The transformer might be better on average but worse for a specific equipment/region combination. Mitigation: the drift dashboard gets per-segment MAE panels. (Note added 2026-05-12: this risk materialised in INC-2026-019. The promotion checklist now blocks any segment regressing by more than 10%.)
- **Explainability.** SHAP-style explanations are harder. We provide attention-based feature importances in the internal "why this ETA" panel for dispatchers only.
- **Cost.** Roughly $2,100/month more in compute for serving and training.

## Consequences

The console team (Lena Brandt) ships the confidence-band UI behind the same regional flag, so dispatchers in a region see the band only once that region is served by v4. Customer-facing shipper notifications continue to quote only the P50 value, rounded to the nearest 15 minutes, because product felt a range would generate more support tickets than it prevents.

ADR-014 is superseded. New feature work targets the `eta-tft` family only; the GBM codepath will be deleted from `ml/eta-predictor` once the 90-day rollback window closes (planned for 2026-07-15, ticket ATLAS-2877).

documents.title: ADR-025: Terraform changes applied only through Atlantis
documents.summary: All changes to atlas-infra are planned and applied via Atlantis PR comments; local applies against prod are forbidden.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Tomasz Wierzbicki.

Local `terraform apply` from laptops caused two state-lock collisions and one accidental destroy in staging. From now on, `atlas-infra` changes are planned and applied through Atlantis (`atlantis plan -p <project>` / `atlantis apply -p <project>` as PR comments). Prod projects require an approving review from the platform team before apply. Humans keep read-only AWS roles in prod; the Atlantis role is the only principal with write access.

documents.title: ADR-026: Money stored as integer minor units with currency
documents.summary: All monetary amounts are int64 minor units plus an ISO 4217 currency code; floats are forbidden.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Hannah Kowalczyk.

After a rounding discrepancy of $0.01 on about 3% of multi-line invoices, all money in Atlas is represented as `int64` minor units (cents for USD, CAD, MXN) plus a 3-letter ISO 4217 code. In Postgres: `amount_minor bigint NOT NULL, currency char(3) NOT NULL`. In protobufs: the shared `atlas.money.v1.Money` message. In TypeScript: the `Money` type from `@nwf/atlas-money`, formatted only at the view layer. Currency conversion happens once, at invoice finalisation, using the daily rate snapshot in `billing.fx_rates`.

Scope of the change: the `billing` schema was migrated in April 2025 (columns renamed from `amount numeric(12,2)` to `amount_minor bigint`), rate-engine outputs were converted the same month, and the console switched to `@nwf/atlas-money` in May. Any remaining `numeric` money column found in a review should be treated as a bug. The decision was prompted by INC-2025-012. Currencies with zero minor units (JPY) or three (KWD) are not supported today; the `money` package rejects them explicitly so that nobody assumes two decimals by accident.

documents.title: ADR-027: PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode for all services
documents.summary: Application pods connect to Aurora through PgBouncer in transaction mode to cap connection counts.
documents.body:
**Status:** Accepted. Owner: Yusuf Demir.

With ~180 pods each holding a pool of 10 connections, the Aurora writer was hitting its `max_connections` of 2,000 during deploys when old and new pods overlapped. We run PgBouncer 1.22 as a 3-replica deployment in the `atlas` namespace, transaction pooling, `default_pool_size=40` per database/user pair.

Consequences for developers:
- No session state: no `SET` without `SET LOCAL`, no session advisory locks, no `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, no prepared statements outside pgx's `QueryExecModeCacheDescribe`.
- Anything that needs session features (outbox-relay's leader lock, goose migrations) connects to the writer directly on 5432.
- In staging PgBouncer is not deployed; services connect directly. Code that accidentally depends on session state will therefore pass in staging and fail in prod — the integration suite runs against a PgBouncer container to catch this.

Monitoring: the "Atlas / Postgres (Aurora)" dashboard has a PgBouncer row showing `cl_waiting` per pool. Sustained waiting clients above 20 means a pool is too small or a service is holding transactions open across network calls, which code review should have caught.

documents.title: Go error wrapping with pkg/errors
documents.summary: Go services wrap errors with github.com/pkg/errors and log stack traces at the boundary.
documents.body: Rule for Go code in `services/`: wrap every returned error with `errors.Wrap(err, "context")` or `errors.Wrapf` from `github.com/pkg/errors` so the stack trace is captured where the error first crosses a package boundary. At the handler, log with `%+v` to print the stack. Do not wrap an error twice in the same function. Sentinel errors are declared with `errors.New` in an `errors.go` file per package.

documents.title: Go errors: stdlib wrapping with %w, pkg/errors banned
documents.summary: Use fmt.Errorf with %w, errors.Is/As and errors.Join; pkg/errors is removed. Supersedes conv-go-errors-pkg-errors.

documents.title: Pull requests need two approvals
documents.summary: Every PR to northwind/atlas requires two approving reviews before merge.
documents.body: Branch protection on `main` in `northwind/atlas` requires two approving reviews, passing CI and a linear history (squash merge only). Authors may not approve their own PRs and a push after approval dismisses stale reviews. Aim to review within one business day; ping in the team channel if a PR waits longer.

documents.title: PR approval policy: one approval, CODEOWNER required on critical paths
documents.summary: PRs now need one approval, which must come from a CODEOWNER for critical paths; supersedes the two-approval rule.
documents.body:
Supersedes `conv-pr-two-approvals`.

Two approvals were slowing small changes without catching more bugs (review data from Q4 2025 showed the second reviewer left substantive comments on 6% of PRs). New policy, effective 2026-01-19:

- **Default:** one approving review from anyone on the engineering team.
- **Critical paths:** if the PR touches a path marked `# critical` in `.github/CODEOWNERS` — currently `services/billing-svc/`, `services/dispatch-svc/internal/tender/`, `proto/`, `deploy/envs/prod/`, and any `migrations/` directory — the approval must come from a listed code owner.
- **Migrations and money** still require a second approval from the owning team, enforced by the `require-second-review` GitHub Action.
- Squash merge only, stale approvals dismissed on push (unchanged).

Proposed by Kevin Liu; agreed in the architecture review of 2026-01-08.

Practical notes:
- The CODEOWNERS file maps billing paths to `@northwind/atlas-billing` (Seun Adeyemi is the primary), tender code to `@northwind/atlas-dispatch` (Priya Raman), `proto/` to `@northwind/atlas-api-guild`, and prod deploy values to `@northwind/platform`.
- Emergency fixes during an incident may be merged with one approval from any on-call engineer using the `incident-bypass` label; the label triggers a follow-up review ticket automatically.
- Review turnaround expectations are unchanged: one business day.

documents.title: Go logging conventions (log/slog)
documents.summary: Go services log JSON through log/slog with a fixed set of field names and no PII.
documents.body:
All Go services use the standard library `log/slog` with the JSON handler, created by `platform/logging.New(serviceName)`. Conventions:

- Levels: `DEBUG` (off in prod), `INFO` for state changes, `WARN` for recoverable anomalies, `ERROR` only when someone may need to act.
- Standard keys: `svc`, `env`, `trace_id`, `span_id`, `load_id`, `carrier_id`, `atl_code` (e.g. `ATL-5102`), `err`.
- Use `slog.With` on a request-scoped logger from `logging.FromContext(ctx)` instead of repeating fields.
- Never log driver phone numbers, emails or full addresses; use IDs. The `piiscan` linter flags common field names like `phone`.
- One log line per request at the end (access log) is emitted by middleware; don't add your own "request started" lines.

Logs go to stdout and are shipped to Loki; the Loki label set is limited to `svc`, `env`, `level`, and `namespace`.

A typical query to find all capacity rejections for one carrier in the last hour:

```
{svc="dispatch-svc", env="prod"} | json | atl_code="ATL-4012" | carrier_id="car_8812"
```

If you need a field to be searchable, keep it a JSON key, not a Loki label; labels with high cardinality make Loki ingestion fall over.

documents.title: Ops console logging conventions (TypeScript)
documents.summary: The React ops console logs through a shared logger that feeds Sentry breadcrumbs; console.log is banned.
documents.body:
In `web/ops-console`, never call `console.log` directly (ESLint `no-console` is an error). Import `logger` from `src/lib/logger.ts`:

- `logger.debug` — dev only, stripped from production builds.
- `logger.info` — becomes a Sentry breadcrumb, not an event.
- `logger.warn` — breadcrumb plus a counter in the RUM dashboard.
- `logger.error(err, context)` — creates a Sentry event with the gateway's `trace_id` if the error came from an API response.

Context objects use camelCase keys (`loadId`, `carrierId`, `atlCode`) — note the difference from the Go services, which use snake_case (`load_id`). Do not include user emails or driver phone numbers; the Sentry `beforeSend` hook scrubs fields named `email` or `phone` but don't rely on it.

Sentry project: `ops-console` in the `northwind` org, with releases tagged by the git SHA injected at build time as `VITE_ATLAS_RELEASE`. Source maps are uploaded in CI and are never served publicly. Errors from the API client are grouped by `atlCode` via a fingerprint rule, so a burst of ATL-4012 errors shows up as one issue rather than hundreds.

documents.title: Commit message and branch naming rules
documents.summary: Conventional Commits with a Jira key; branches named type/ATLAS-1234-short-desc.
documents.body:
- Branches: `<type>/ATLAS-<ticket>-<short-kebab-desc>`, e.g. `fix/ATLAS-1642-tracking-rebalance`.
- Squash-commit titles follow Conventional Commits with scope = service: `fix(tracking-svc): use cooperative-sticky assignor (ATLAS-1642)`.
- Types: `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`, `build`, `ci`.
- Breaking API changes add `!` after the scope and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.

Release notes are generated from these titles, so write them for an operator, not for yourself.

documents.title: Go code review handbook for Atlas services
documents.summary: The full checklist reviewers apply to Go changes in Atlas: context, errors, database, Kafka, tests and observability.
documents.body:
This handbook is what reviewers actually look at when approving a Go PR in `services/`. It is maintained by Priya Raman and was last reworked after the error-handling migration in September 2025. If a rule here conflicts with an older memory, this one wins. Nothing in it replaces judgement; it exists so that review comments are consistent and so that authors can self-check before asking for review.

## 0. Before requesting review

- `make lint test` passes locally. CI runs `golangci-lint` with the repo's `.golangci.yml` (govet, staticcheck, errcheck, gosec, depguard, revive, piiscan, and our custom `atlasctx` analyzer).
