- **2026-02-11 01:52** — The nightly carrier adjustment import runs. One row in a carrier-supplied CSV contains `US D` in the currency column. The import validates the amount but not the currency; the value flows into a ledger event.
- **01:52** — `billing-ledger-writer` pod owning partition 7 begins failing with `money: unknown currency "US D"`. It retries every 500 ms. Logs show roughly 7,000 identical errors per hour.
- **02:00–10:30** — Lag on partition 7 grows slowly (billing volume is low overnight). Total lag never exceeds 3,500 messages. No alert fires.
- **07:30** — Finance's first AR analyst notices some balances look stale; assumes a normal overnight delay.
- **10:40** — Finance escalates in #atlas-billing. Seun Adeyemi checks "Atlas / Kafka Consumer Lag", sees partition 7 flat at the same offset since 01:52.
- **10:48** — Seun pages Samir Haddad (Kafka ops) and declares SEV-2. #inc-2026-008 opened.
- **11:02** — `atlasctl kafka sample billing.ledger.v1 --partition 7 --offset 5518842 --count 1` shows the bad currency.
- **11:10** — Debate about options. Skipping the offset (resetting to 5518843) is rejected: every ledger event must be applied, and skipping would silently leave an account balance wrong. Editing the message is impossible in Kafka.
- **11:25** — Decision: hotfix the consumer to route unparseable events to a DLQ topic and continue, then correct the bad event with a compensating ledger entry.
- **11:30** — Samir creates `billing.ledger.v1.dlq` via an emergency Atlantis apply (DLQ topics existed for other domains but not yet for billing — ATLAS-2411).
- **12:05** — Hotfix `billing-svc@c7720f3` built. Merged with the `incident-bypass` label and one on-call approval.
- **12:20** — Hotfix deployed to `billing-ledger-writer`. The bad event goes to the DLQ after 3 attempts; partition 7 starts draining.
- **12:47** — Lag at zero. Seun posts a compensating ledger pair (reversal of the malformed event and a corrected event in `USD`) via `atlasctl billing ledger correct --event <id> --currency USD`.
- **13:30** — Invoice finalisation re-run for affected accounts. 611 invoices finalised.
- **14:00** — AR report regenerated. Incident resolved.

## Root cause

1. **Missing validation at the edge.** The carrier adjustment importer accepted a free-text currency value. The `platform/money` package validates currency codes when constructing a `Money` value, but the importer built the ledger event protobuf directly from strings, bypassing the constructor.
2. **Infinite retry in the consumer.** `billing-ledger-writer` treated every processing error as transient and retried forever. There was no dead-letter path for billing, on the reasoning that "billing must never drop an event". But a message that can never be processed is not made safer by blocking everything behind it.
3. **Alerting on the wrong signal.** The lag threshold was calibrated in message counts, copied from higher-volume groups. For billing, the meaningful signal is the age of the oldest unprocessed message.

## Why this was not like the tracking incident

People reached for the tracking playbook first — "scale out, check for rebalances". For a poison message, scaling does nothing (one partition, one consumer), and offset resets are forbidden. The new billing lag runbook explicitly separates these cases, and it is intentionally a different document from the tracking runbook even though the titles look similar.

## What went well

- The append-only ledger made recovery clean: nothing needed to be edited, only compensated.
- Refusing to skip the offset avoided a silent balance error that might have surfaced months later in an audit.
- Seun, who was a week into shadowing the billing ownership, drove the investigation effectively.

## Action items

| # | Action | Owner | Ticket | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Consumers route to `<topic>.dlq` after 3 failures via `kafkax.WithDLQ`; mandatory for all new consumers (review handbook updated) | Samir Haddad | ATLAS-2410 | Done |
| 2 | Create `billing.ledger.v1.dlq` in Terraform (not emergency apply) and audit that every topic has a DLQ | Tomasz Wierzbicki | ATLAS-2411 | Done |
| 3 | Validate all money fields through `money.New` in importers; add a fuzz test for the CSV importer | Seun Adeyemi | ATLAS-2414 | Done |
| 4 | Alert `BillingLedgerLagHigh` on oldest-message age > 15 min or lag > 10,000 | Samir Haddad | ATLAS-2420 | Done |
| 5 | Write the billing consumer lag runbook | Seun Adeyemi | — | Done (runbook-kafka-lag-billing-ledger-writer) |
| 6 | Add `atlasctl billing ledger correct` to the billing runbook set with approval rules | Seun Adeyemi | ATLAS-2425 | Done |
| 7 | DB check constraint `currency ~ '^[A-Z]{3}$'` on `billing.ledger_events` | Yusuf Demir | ATLAS-2426 | Done 2026-03-02 |

## Lessons

"Never drop a message" and "never block on a message" are both correct requirements, and a DLQ plus monitored replay is how you satisfy both. Alert thresholds should be expressed in terms of user impact (age, staleness) rather than copied counts. Finally, validation belongs where untrusted data enters — a carrier's CSV is as untrusted as any public API.

documents.title: INC-2026-019: eta-tft-4.0.0 badly late for reefer loads in the Pacific Northwest
documents.summary: Postmortem for the May 2026 ETA incident where a timezone feature bug made the new transformer model predict reefer ETAs hours late in one region.
documents.body:
**Severity:** SEV-3 (no outage; degraded accuracy with customer impact). **Date:** 2026-05-06, detected 2026-05-06 16:20 UTC, mitigated 17:05 UTC, fixed model promoted 2026-05-11. **Incident commander:** Kevin Liu. **Owning team:** ML (Farah Nadeem). **Tickets:** ATLAS-2791, ATLAS-2792, ATLAS-2795, ATLAS-2801.

## Summary

The `eta-tft-4.0.0` transformer model (ADR-024) was rolled out region by region through April and reached the Pacific Northwest/West region on 2026-05-04. Two days later, customer success escalated complaints from three grocery shippers that ETAs for refrigerated deliveries into Seattle, Portland and Vancouver distribution centres were consistently predicting next-morning arrival for trucks that arrived the same afternoon. Investigation found that the `appointment_local_hour` feature was computed differently in training and serving for facilities in Pacific timezones, off by exactly one hour since the start of daylight saving time. The model had learned that reefer receiving windows at cold-storage DCs close sharply, so a one-hour shift pushed many predictions outside the window and onto the next day. Aggregate metrics barely moved; the segment was small.

## Impact

- Segment MAE for reefer × Pacific Northwest/West rose from 11 minutes (shadow period estimate) to 38 minutes; for loads with appointments within 90 minutes of a receiving-window close, the median error was over 9 hours.
- Aggregate MAE across all loads moved only from 11.2 to 12.9 minutes, which was below the drift alert threshold.
- About 1,450 shipper-facing "delivery at risk" notifications were sent incorrectly across 2 days. Three shippers escalated; one grocery customer temporarily disabled Atlas ETA notifications for its receiving team.
- Dispatchers in the West region re-planned 37 driver relays based on wrong P90 values before the problem was understood.

## Timeline (UTC)

- **2026-03-01** — Training/evaluation snapshot for `eta-tft-4.0.0` frozen for reproducibility.
- **2026-03-08** — US daylight saving time begins.
- **2026-03-16 to 03-30** — Shadow period. Per-segment shadow metrics were computed only for the three largest regions to save compute; the West region was not included.
- **2026-04-02** — ADR-024 accepted. Regional rollout begins via `atlas.eta.model-v4-regions`: Southeast (04-06), Midwest (04-14), Northeast and South Central (04-21), Mountain (04-28), Pacific Northwest/West (05-04).
- **2026-05-06 15:10** — Customer success opens a ticket about Seattle reefer ETAs.
- **16:20** — Ticket reaches Farah Nadeem, who confirms on "ML / ETA Model Drift" that the reefer/West segment panel (added only for three regions) is missing, and pulls numbers manually. Declares an incident.
- **16:35** — Kevin Liu takes IC. Options discussed: force fallback globally (would degrade every region), roll back globally, or remove West from the rollout flag.
- **16:50** — Jonah Pierce removes `pnw-west` from `atlas.eta.model-v4-regions`. West loads go back to `eta-gbm-3.2.1` via `ETA_SECONDARY_MODEL_URI`.
- **17:05** — Next eta-publisher cycle completes; West reefer MAE returns to ~17 min (GBM level). Mitigated.
- **2026-05-07** — Root cause identified by Marcus Oyelaran and Jonah: in the training feature pipeline, `appointment_local_hour` was derived with a static offset table (`facility_utc_offsets.csv`) built in January; serving uses proper IANA zones via `zoneinfo`. After 03-08, every Pacific facility's feature was off by one hour between training and serving. Eastern and Central facilities used the same table, but their offset table had been regenerated in March by an unrelated fix, so only Pacific and Mountain entries were stale. Mountain showed a smaller effect because fewer facilities there have strict receiving windows.
- **2026-05-08** — `eta-tft-4.0.1` trained with IANA-based features; failed the new segment check on flatbed/Mountain (a different, unrelated regression from a data refresh).
- **2026-05-10** — `eta-tft-4.0.2` built with a fix to the data refresh; an integration test caught that the feature builder still wrote `schema_version=4.0` for a changed feature. Not promoted.
- **2026-05-11** — `eta-tft-4.0.3` passes all segment checks (no segment worse than production by more than 10%) and a 24-hour abbreviated shadow on West traffic. Promoted; West re-enabled.

## Root cause

Training/serving skew in a timezone-derived feature. The feature definitions in `ml/eta-predictor/features/` were meant to be shared between training and serving, but `appointment_local_hour` had a training-only fast path added in January for performance (vectorised pandas instead of per-row `zoneinfo` conversion) which used a static offset table. The shared-definition rule was violated without anyone noticing because the tests compared outputs only for dates in winter.

## Contributing factors

1. **Aggregate metrics hid a segment regression.** The drift alert fires on aggregate MAE over 15 minutes or fallback share over 20%, and the promotion checklist looked only at aggregate holdout MAE.
2. **Incomplete shadow coverage.** Per-segment shadow metrics for only three regions.
3. **Evaluation snapshot predated DST.** The frozen snapshot meant the holdout contained no post-DST weeks.
4. **No timezone rule in ML code.** The Go services had "store UTC, convert only at display" as a convention; ML code did not follow it.

## What went well

- The regional rollout flag made mitigation surgical: one region reverted in 15 minutes without touching the others.
- Keeping `eta-gbm-3.2.1` loadable (ADR-024's 90-day rollback window) paid off.
- The segment check caught two further bad candidates (4.0.1, 4.0.2) before they reached production.

## Action items

| # | Action | Owner | Ticket | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Remove the training-only fast path; all timezone features use IANA zones in both paths | Jonah Pierce | ATLAS-2791 | Done |
| 2 | Promotion checklist: no segment (equipment × region, 18 segments) may regress by more than 10% | Farah Nadeem | ATLAS-2792 | Done |
| 3 | Drift dashboard shows all 18 segments; alert when any segment MAE exceeds 45 min | Farah Nadeem | ATLAS-2795 | Done |
| 4 | Golden-file tests include dates on both sides of DST transitions (March and November) | Jonah Pierce | ATLAS-2801 | Done |
| 5 | Timezone convention extended to `ml/` code | Priya Raman | — | Done (conv-timestamps-utc) |
| 6 | Write the ETA model rollback runbook | Farah Nadeem | — | Done (runbook-eta-model-rollback) |
| 7 | Suppress "delivery at risk" shipper notifications when P90 − P50 exceeds 4 hours (uncertain prediction) | Aiko Tanabe | ATLAS-2810 | In progress |

## Lessons

A better model on average can still be worse where it matters. We now treat per-segment evaluation as a release gate rather than a dashboard nicety, and we treat every feature involving local time as suspect around DST boundaries. The fixed production model as of this writing is `eta-tft-4.0.3`.

documents.title: INC-2025-005: 312 duplicate tenders from carrier API retries
documents.summary: Carrier integrations retried timed-out tender accepts, creating duplicate tenders; led to ADR-022 idempotency keys.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-02-14. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Priya Raman.

During a Friday afternoon slowdown in dispatch (p99 at 3 s from a missing index on `dispatch.tenders(load_id, status)`), two large carrier integrations timed out at 2 seconds and retried tender creation and acceptance calls. Over the week the retries created 312 duplicate tenders and 41 loads double-assigned to the same carrier. Dispatchers cleaned up by hand. Fixes: the index (ATLAS-1102), and ADR-022 introducing mandatory `Idempotency-Key` headers for partner write calls. Also the origin of Priya's rule of no dispatch deploys after 14:00 ET on Fridays.

documents.title: INC-2025-009: staging Prometheus OOM from a load_id metric label
documents.summary: A metric labelled by load_id created 2 million series and crashed staging Prometheus.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-03-18. **Severity:** SEV-4 (staging only).

A new histogram `dispatch_tender_latency_seconds{load_id=...}` was merged to staging. Within six hours it produced about 2 million active series and Prometheus in staging was OOM-killed repeatedly, taking staging alerting with it. Reverted the same day. Outcome: the metric naming convention now forbids IDs as labels, and a `promtool`-based cardinality check in CI rejects label names `load_id`, `truck_id`, `carrier_id` and `user_id`.

documents.title: INC-2025-012: one-cent discrepancies on multi-line invoices
documents.summary: Floating-point arithmetic in fuel surcharge calculation produced $0.01 errors on about 3% of invoices.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-04-03. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Hannah Kowalczyk.

A large shipper's AP team reported that invoice totals differed by $0.01 from the sum of lines on some invoices. Investigation found fuel surcharge lines computed with `float64` and rounded per line, while the total was computed from unrounded values. About 3% of multi-line invoices since January were affected (4,218 invoices, total drift $31.07). Corrected invoices were reissued. Led directly to ADR-026 (money as int64 minor units) and the `platform/money` package.

documents.title: INC-2025-014: Terraform security-group change blocked eta-predictor model loading
documents.summary: An inline security-group rule replacement removed S3 endpoint egress for the ML node group; ETAs ran on fallback for 47 minutes.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-04-09. **Severity:** SEV-3. **IC:** Samir Haddad. **Owners:** Tomasz Wierzbicki (platform), Farah Nadeem (ML).

**What happened.** An Atlantis apply to `prod-network` added an ingress rule to the ML node group's security group. The security group used inline `ingress {}` / `egress {}` blocks, and the plan showed the group's rules being replaced in place. For about 40 seconds during the apply the egress rule to the S3 gateway prefix list was missing, and a separate egress rule added manually in the console months earlier (never in Terraform) was removed permanently. That manual rule allowed HTTPS to the MLflow artifact proxy.

At 14:12 UTC, a scheduled node rotation restarted the eta-api pods. They could not download model artifacts from `s3://nwf-ml-models/eta/` via the proxy, and with `ETA_FALLBACK_MODE=serve` they started successfully but served rules-based ETAs. `atlas_eta_fallback_total{reason="model_unavailable"}` jumped to 100%.

**Detection.** The "Atlas ML" PagerDuty service paged at 14:27 (fallback share > 20% for 15 minutes). ML on-call found `AccessDenied`/timeout errors in eta-api startup logs.

**Mitigation.** 14:59: the missing egress rule was re-added via Atlantis; eta-api restarted; model loaded at 15:01. Total fallback time: 47 minutes. Customer impact was limited to less accurate ETAs (fallback MAE ~26 min).

**Action items.**
- Ban inline security-group rule blocks; use standalone rule resources (Terraform conventions updated) — Tomasz, ATLAS-1231.
- Detect console-created drift: nightly `terraform plan` on all prod projects posting drift to #atlas-platform — Tomasz, ATLAS-1232.
- Alert on eta-api startup model-load failures directly, not just via fallback share — Farah, ATLAS-1235.
- Document the force-fallback lever for general on-call — done (runbook-force-eta-fallback).

documents.title: INC-2025-016: Aurora max_connections exhausted during overlapping deploys
documents.summary: Two concurrent Jenkins deploys doubled pod counts and exhausted Aurora connections; led to PgBouncer adoption.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-04-24. **Severity:** SEV-2, 11 minutes. **Owner:** Yusuf Demir.

Dispatch and billing were deployed at the same time via Jenkins. During the rolling updates, old and new pods overlapped, each opening a 10-connection pool, and the Aurora writer hit `max_connections` (2,000). New connections failed with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`; tender creation returned 500s for 11 minutes. Follow-up: ADR-027 introduced PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode and a limit of one concurrent prod deploy per database in the deploy process.

documents.title: INC-2025-019: ops console blank screen after release
documents.summary: CloudFront cached an old index.html pointing at deleted asset chunks; dispatchers saw a blank page for 25 minutes.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-05-27. **Severity:** SEV-2 (dispatch floor blocked), 25 minutes. **Owner:** Lena Brandt.

The console release workflow deleted previous asset chunks from S3 while CloudFront was still serving a cached `index.html` (TTL 1 hour) that referenced them. Users loading the page got `ChunkLoadError` and a blank screen. Fixed by invalidating `/index.html`. Follow-ups: `index.html` served with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, the workflow keeps the previous two releases' assets, and the runbook `runbook-ops-console-cloudfront-invalidation` was written.

documents.title: INC-2025-027: Argo CD re-deployed a rolled-back rate-engine version
documents.summary: A manual rollback without a Git revert was undone by the next sync, re-deploying the broken release.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-07-02. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Tomasz Wierzbicki.

A rate-engine release returned wrong fuel surcharges. On-call rolled back with `kubectl argo rollouts undo`, which fixed it, but didn't revert the prod values PR. Forty minutes later someone synced an unrelated change to `atlas-apps`, Argo CD reconciled rate-engine to the desired state in Git — the bad version — and the problem returned for 18 minutes. The deploy runbook now says in bold to revert Git immediately after any manual rollback, and `atlasctl release revert` was added to make that a one-liner.

documents.title: INC-2025-036: carriers wrongly rejected with ATL-4012
documents.summary: Expired tenders were not decrementing carrier capacity, so carriers hit the open-tender limit falsely.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-08-14. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Priya Raman.

After a refactor of the tender expiry loop (ATLAS-1702), tenders moving `OFFERED → EXPIRED` no longer decremented `dispatch.carrier_capacity.open_tenders`. Over three days, high-volume carriers accumulated phantom open tenders until they hit `DISPATCH_MAX_TENDERS_PER_CARRIER` (25) and every new tender failed with ATL-4012. Dispatchers first assumed the carriers were genuinely at capacity — ATL-4012 is often confused with ATL-4013 (carrier suspended), and some tried to "unsuspend" carriers that were never suspended.

Fix: decrement moved into the same SQL statement as the status transition, plus a nightly reconciliation job `carrier-capacity-reconcile` that recomputes counts from `dispatch.tenders` and logs any drift. 188 carriers had counts corrected.

Detection took three days because ATL-4012 is a normal, expected response and nobody alerted on its rate. The dispatch golden-signals dashboard now has a panel for ATL-4012 per carrier, and an alert fires if more than 20 distinct carriers hit the limit within an hour, which historically never happens organically.

documents.title: INC-2025-040: drivers texted wrong pickup times
documents.summary: A template change rendered pickup times in UTC instead of facility-local time for about 1,100 drivers.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-09-10. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Aiko Tanabe.

A notify-svc template refactor dropped the `facilityTime` helper, so pickup reminders showed UTC times (e.g. "pickup at 14:00" for a 10:00 ET appointment). About 1,100 drivers received wrong times over 3 hours; 19 arrived early and waited. Because notify-svc was on RabbitMQ at the time, the corrected messages could not be replayed from the broker and had to be regenerated from dispatch data with a one-off script. This was one of the motivations for ADR-019. Template tests now render every template with a non-UTC facility.

documents.title: INC-2025-044: Twilio throttling delayed driver SMS by up to 70 minutes
documents.summary: Twilio 20429 throttling during the morning rush backed up notify-svc; no failover procedure existed.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-10-06. **Severity:** SEV-2. **IC:** Samir Haddad. **Owner:** Aiko Tanabe.

**What happened.** At 11:05 UTC (07:05 ET, the dispatch rush), Twilio began returning error `20429 Too Many Requests` for our messaging service. A marketing campaign run by another Northwind business unit had been configured on the same Twilio account and consumed most of the account-level throughput. notify-svc retried with delays, the RabbitMQ queue `notify-dispatcher` grew to 48,000 messages, and pickup reminders arrived up to 70 minutes late.

**Detection.** Driver complaints to carrier ops at 11:40. There was no alert on SMS failure rate, and the RabbitMQ queue-depth graph lived in a separate "Notify / RabbitMQ" dashboard that the on-call engineer did not find for about 20 minutes.

**Mitigation.** Aiko hand-edited notify-svc config to route SMS through Sinch (a contract existed but had never been used in prod), deployed at 12:30, and the queue drained by 13:15.

**Action items.**
- Separate Twilio subaccount for Atlas with dedicated throughput — Aiko, ATLAS-1850.
- Unleash flag `atlas.notify.sms-provider` for instant provider switch; runbook `runbook-sms-provider-failover` — Aiko, ATLAS-1851.
- Alert on SMS failure ratio > 5% for 5 min — Samir, ATLAS-1852.
- Consider moving notify to Kafka to consolidate dashboards and on-call knowledge — became ADR-019.

documents.title: INC-2025-055: staging MSK brokers ran out of disk
documents.summary: A load test left 3 TB of synthetic telemetry in staging Kafka; brokers filled up and staging was down for half a day.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2025-12-04. **Severity:** SEV-4 (staging).

A load test for peak season published synthetic pings to staging `telemetry.gps.v2` at prod rates for 9 hours. Staging topics had retention set to 7 days (the prod value is 72 h), so broker EBS volumes (1 TB each) filled and the staging MSK cluster stopped accepting writes. All staging consumers stalled; the e2e suite failed for the afternoon. Fix: staging retention aligned with prod, MSK storage autoscaling enabled for staging, and load tests must use a dedicated `loadtest.` topic prefix with 6-hour retention.

documents.title: INC-2026-003: docs-svc internal certificate expired
documents.summary: A manually issued TLS certificate on docs-svc's internal ingress expired, breaking POD uploads and blocking invoicing for 3 hours.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2026-01-19. **Severity:** SEV-2. **IC:** Kevin Liu. **Owner:** platform (Tomasz Wierzbicki) with billing.

**What happened.** docs-svc's internal ingress `docs.nwf.internal` used a certificate issued by hand from the private CA in January 2025, before the cert-manager rollout, with a 1-year validity. It expired at 00:00 UTC on 2026-01-19, a US holiday. Driver app uploads of proof-of-delivery photos go through the gateway, which calls docs-svc over that ingress for presigned URLs; the gateway rejected the expired certificate, so uploads failed with 502s.

Because billing only invoices automatically when a POD reference exists, invoices for 2,300 delivered loads were held. Drivers saw an upload error and many simply closed the app; about 600 PODs needed to be collected again from carriers.

**Detection.** 03:10 UTC via a spike in 502s on "Atlas / Dispatch Golden Signals" (upload route) — the certificate-expiry alert only covered cert-manager `Certificate` resources, and this one wasn't one.

**Mitigation.** 03:40: a `Certificate` resource was created for the ingress and cert-manager issued a new certificate in 2 minutes. Uploads recovered immediately; held invoices were processed by 06:00 once PODs arrived.

**Action items.**
- `cert-audit` job fails CI for any TLS secret not owned by cert-manager — Tomasz, ATLAS-2301.
- Blackbox exporter probes for every `*.nwf.internal` host, alerting at 14 days to expiry regardless of issuer — Samir, ATLAS-2302.
- Driver app: queue failed POD uploads and retry for 24 h instead of showing an error — mobile team, ATLAS-2305.

documents.title: INC-2026-012: appointment windows shown an hour off after DST
documents.summary: The ops console displayed appointment windows one hour off for Arizona facilities after the March DST change.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2026-03-09. **Severity:** SEV-4. **Owner:** Lena Brandt.

After DST began on 2026-03-08, dispatchers noticed appointment windows for Phoenix and Tucson facilities displayed an hour late in the console. Those facilities were stored with `facility_tz = 'America/Denver'` instead of `America/Phoenix` (Arizona does not observe DST). 43 facilities were corrected with a data migration, and facility creation now suggests the timezone from coordinates via the timezone boundary dataset. No ETA or billing impact because services use stored UTC instants.

documents.title: INC-2026-015: missing ping partition slowed tracking ingest
documents.summary: The partman maintenance CronJob failed silently, pings landed in the default partition and tracking-ingest lagged.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2026-04-07. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Marcus Oyelaran.

The `partman-maintenance` CronJob had been failing for 8 days with an `ImagePullBackOff` after its image tag was garbage-collected from ECR. Pre-created partitions ran out on 2026-04-07, and pings went into `tracking.gps_pings_default`, which lacks the BRIN index; COPY latency rose from 150 ms to 4 s and `tracking-ingest` lag reached 1.2M. Fixed by running maintenance manually and moving rows (see `runbook-backfill-tracking-partition`). Follow-ups: ECR lifecycle rule excludes images referenced by CronJobs; alert on `kube_job_status_failed` for any CronJob in `atlas`; alert when fewer than 3 future partitions exist.

documents.title: INC-2026-024: dispatch writes failed for 6 minutes after Aurora failover
documents.summary: PgBouncer kept server connections to the demoted Aurora writer after a maintenance failover, causing read-only errors.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2026-06-30. **Severity:** SEV-2. **IC:** Samir Haddad. **Owner:** Yusuf Demir.

**What happened.** AWS applied a mandatory Aurora minor-version patch at 10:02 UTC on a Tuesday. The cluster's AWS maintenance window had been left at its default instead of our agreed Sunday 06:00–08:00 ET window. The patch triggered a writer failover from `atlas-prod-1` to `atlas-prod-3`, which completed in 38 seconds.

PgBouncer, however, kept its existing server connections to `atlas-prod-1`, which was now a reader. Its `server_check_query` (`select 1`) succeeds on a reader, so the connections were considered healthy and reused. Every write through PgBouncer failed with SQLSTATE 25006 `cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction`. PgBouncer's `dns_max_ttl` had been set to 3600 years earlier, so even new server connections resolved to the old IP.

Dispatch tender creation and acceptance failed for 6 minutes (10:02–10:08). Billing saw a burst of ATL-5102 errors. outbox-relay, which connects directly with pgx, recovered on its own.

**Mitigation.** Samir restarted PgBouncer at 10:07 after recognising the error in dispatch logs; writes recovered at 10:08.

**Action items.**
- `dns_max_ttl = 15`, `server_lifetime = 300`, and `server_check_query` changed to `select pg_is_in_recovery()` with a wrapper that closes connections to readers — Yusuf, ATLAS-3012.
- Align the Aurora maintenance window to Sunday 06:00–08:00 ET in Terraform — Tomasz, ATLAS-3013.
- Rewrite the failover runbook with an explicit PgBouncer `RECONNECT` step — Yusuf, done (runbook-aurora-postgres-failover).
- 142 tenders expired during the window; dispatch re-tendered them manually. Add `atlasctl dispatch tenders expired --since` — Priya, ATLAS-3016.

documents.title: INC-2026-029: EDI 990 responses from three carriers not received
documents.summary: An SFTP host key rotation on a carrier VAN broke edi-bridge polling; tender responses were missing for 14 hours.
documents.body:
**Date:** 2026-08-18. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Owner:** Priya Raman (edi-bridge).

A value-added network used by three mid-size carriers rotated its SFTP host key without notice. edi-bridge's strict host-key checking rejected the connection, and because the error was logged at `WARN` and retried every 5 minutes, nothing alerted. For 14 hours, 990 tender responses from those carriers were not picked up; their tenders expired after 600 seconds and dispatchers re-tendered 212 loads to other carriers, some at higher cost. Fixes: alert when any SFTP partner has had no successful poll in 60 minutes (`atlas_edi_sftp_last_success_seconds`), host keys moved to a reviewed config with a documented rotation procedure, and an `ERROR` log on host-key mismatch.

The affected carriers' SCACs were configured in `services/edi-bridge/partners/` with host keys pinned in the partner YAML. After the fix, host-key changes are applied by PR to those files with a second reviewer from platform, and the VAN's published key fingerprints are checked by a weekly job.

documents.title: Atlas team roster and ownership matrix
documents.summary: Who owns which Atlas service, dependency and process as of April 2026, with backups, channels and working hours.
documents.body:
This is the canonical "who do I ask" memory for Atlas, refreshed after the billing ownership change in March 2026. When a memory about an individual disagrees with this one, check dates: this was accurate on 2026-04-01.

## Leadership

- **Rosalind Achebe** — CTO. Final approver for regional DR failover and for any ADR that changes a data store or messaging system. Holds a monthly "Atlas health" review on the first Wednesday.
- **Kevin Liu** — Engineering Manager for Core Logistics (dispatch, tracking, pricing, billing, notify). Runs sprint planning on Mondays, owns the incident review process, and is the default incident commander for SEV-1s during business hours.
- **Mei-Ling Zhou** — Product Manager for dispatch and carrier experience. Decides on bulk re-tendering after outages and signs off on anything that changes what shippers or carriers see.

## Service ownership

| Service / area | Primary owner | Backup | Slack channel |
|---|---|---|---|
| dispatch-svc, tender logic, edi-bridge | Priya Raman | Diego Salvatierra | #atlas-dispatch |
| tracking-svc, tracking-ingest, telemetry pipeline | Marcus Oyelaran | Samir Haddad | #atlas-tracking |
| rate-engine | Diego Salvatierra | Priya Raman | #atlas-pricing |
| billing-svc, ledger, invoicing | Seun Adeyemi | Yusuf Demir | #atlas-billing |

| ops-console | Lena Brandt | Nadia Petrov (contract, a11y only) | #atlas-console |
| atlasctl | Samir Haddad | Priya Raman | #atlas-platform |

## Platform, data and security

| Area | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Terraform / atlas-infra, EKS clusters, MSK provisioning, Argo CD | Tomasz Wierzbicki | Approves prod Atlantis applies |
| Kafka runtime (topic configs, consumer lag alerts, ACLs in practice), PagerDuty schedules, alert tuning | Samir Haddad | Pair with Tom on anything MSK |
| Aurora Postgres, PgBouncer, partitioning, failovers | Yusuf Demir | Also backup for billing |

The split between Tomasz and Samir is the one people get wrong most often. Rough rule: if the change is in Terraform (creating a topic, changing broker size, adding a cluster), it goes to Tomasz. If it's about how things behave at runtime (a consumer group lagging, retention on an existing topic being too short for an incident, an alert threshold), it goes to Samir. Both review ADRs that touch Kafka.

## On-call

- **Atlas Core Primary** (PagerDuty): weekly rotation among Priya, Marcus, Diego, Aiko, Seun, Samir, Yusuf and Lena. Handoff Tuesdays 10:00 ET.
- **Atlas Billing** (PagerDuty): business hours only, Seun and Yusuf alternating; after hours, billing pages route to the Core primary, who should stabilise and not attempt ledger corrections.
- **Atlas ML** (PagerDuty): Farah and Jonah, business hours; after hours routes to Core primary, whose only expected action is forcing `atlas.eta.force-fallback`.
- Escalation for Kafka: Samir; for Postgres: Yusuf; for anything in Terraform: Tomasz.

## Working hours and locations

- Priya Raman — New York (ET). Core hours 09:00–17:00 ET. No dispatch deploy reviews on Fridays after 14:00 ET.
- Marcus Oyelaran — Atlanta (ET). Often online early (07:00 ET) to watch the morning ping peak.
- Diego Salvatierra — Mexico City (CST, UTC−6 all year). Prefers Spanish or English, equally comfortable.
- Seun Adeyemi — Toronto (ET).
- Aiko Tanabe — Seattle (PT).

- Tomasz Wierzbicki — Kraków (CET/CEST). Atlantis prod applies he approves are usually done before 13:00 ET.
- Samir Haddad — Denver (MT).
- Yusuf Demir — Istanbul (TRT, UTC+3). Maintenance-window failovers on Sunday mornings ET are 13:00–15:00 his time, which he's fine with.

## Meetings that matter

- **Architecture review** — Thursdays 11:00 ET, run by Priya. New ADRs are presented here; send the draft by Tuesday.
- **Incident review** — Wednesdays 12:00 ET, run by Kevin. Every SEV-1/SEV-2 postmortem is read here within 10 business days.
- **Peak season readiness** — weekly from October 1 to Thanksgiving, run by Samir.

## How to reach people

Prefer the service's Slack channel over DMs so answers are searchable. Page only through PagerDuty. For anything security-sensitive (a leaked credential, a suspicious partner token) go straight to Grace Okafor via #security-private or her PagerDuty "Security On-Call" schedule, regardless of time.

documents.title: Rosalind Achebe (CTO) and how to bring her decisions
documents.summary: Rosalind wants one-page written proposals with a clear recommendation and cost, and approves data-store and DR decisions.

She reads everything asynchronously and dislikes slide decks; bring a one-page doc with the recommendation first, alternatives second, and a monthly cost estimate. documents.title: Priya Raman: dispatch owner and review preferences
documents.summary: Priya owns dispatch-svc and edi-bridge, runs architecture review, and wants small async-reviewable PRs.

- PRs under 400 lines, with the "why" in the description. She will ask you to split larger ones.

- No dispatch deploys or deploy reviews on Fridays after 14:00 ET — a rule dating from INC-2025-005.
- Prefers sequence diagrams (Mermaid in the PR) for anything touching tender flows.
- Dislikes new abstractions without two concrete callers.

She owns the Go code review handbook and the `.golangci.yml` config; proposals to add or relax linters go to her. For dispatch incidents she prefers to be paged directly rather than learning about them in the morning, even out of hours, because tender expiry makes dispatch outages time-critical.

documents.title: Production Postgres connection details
documents.summary: Prod services reach Aurora through PgBouncer on port 6432; only migrations and outbox-relay use the writer on 5432.
documents.body:
**Production** (account `atlas-prod`, us-east-1):

- Application DSN host: `pgbouncer.atlas.svc.cluster.local`, **port 6432** (PgBouncer, transaction pooling).
- Read-only pool: `pgbouncer-ro.atlas.svc.cluster.local:6432` → Aurora reader endpoint.
- Aurora writer endpoint (direct, 5432): `atlas-prod.cluster-c8x2k.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com` — used only by `<svc>-migrate` Jobs and outbox-relay.
- Aurora reader endpoint: `atlas-prod.cluster-ro-c8x2k.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432`.
- `sslmode=require` everywhere.
- Credentials: `pg_user` / `pg_password` keys in Secrets Manager `atlas/prod/<svc>`; the DSN is assembled into `ATLAS_PG_DSN` by the Helm chart.

Human access: `atlasctl db psql --db <name> --env prod` (read-only role by default; `--writer` requires `atlas-db-admin`).

documents.title: Staging Postgres connection details
documents.summary: Staging uses a single Aurora instance at atlas-pg-stg.internal:5432 with no PgBouncer; supersedes the old pg-staging-01 host.
documents.body:
Supersedes `env-pg-staging-legacy-host`. The self-managed EC2 box was retired on 2025-09-19.

**Staging** (account `atlas-staging`, us-east-1):

- Host: `atlas-pg-stg.internal` (Route 53 private zone CNAME to the Aurora cluster `atlas-stg`), **port 5432**, direct — there is no PgBouncer in staging.
- Single db.r6g.large instance, Aurora PostgreSQL 15.6 (same major/minor as prod).
- Same database names as prod: `dispatch`, `tracking`, `billing`, `rates`, `notify`, `docs`.
- Credentials: Secrets Manager `atlas/staging/<svc>`, keys `pg_user` / `pg_password`.
- Refreshed weekly (Saturday 04:00 UTC) with anonymised prod data for `dispatch` and `rates` only; `tracking` holds synthetic pings.

Remember the port difference when copying DSNs between environments: prod app traffic is 6432 via PgBouncer, staging is 5432 direct. Code that relies on session state will pass in staging and fail in prod for exactly this reason.

Human access in staging is broader than prod: the `atlas-staging-dev` SSO profile can use `atlasctl db psql --db <name> --env staging --writer` without extra approval. Please still don't run destructive statements during the working day; Ben Thornquist's e2e suite depends on the seeded fixtures, and a broken staging database blocks prod promotions.

documents.title: Staging Postgres host (pg-staging-01)
documents.summary: Staging Postgres runs on the EC2 host pg-staging-01.nwf.local, port 5432, Postgres 13.
documents.body:
Staging databases live on a self-managed EC2 instance: `pg-staging-01.nwf.local:5432`, PostgreSQL 13.11, one database per service. Credentials are in SSM at `/atlas/staging/<svc>/pg_password`. Backups are nightly `pg_dump` to `s3://nwf-staging-backups/pg/`. This box is scheduled to be replaced by Aurora to match prod.

Connect from the office VPN or the staging bastion; the host is not reachable from EKS pods outside the `atlas-staging` VPC.

documents.title: Production Redis (ElastiCache) endpoint
documents.summary: Prod Redis is an ElastiCache cluster-mode endpoint on port 6379 with TLS and AUTH, 7 shards.
documents.body:
- Configuration endpoint: `clustercfg.atlas-redis-prod.x7yq.use1.cache.amazonaws.com`, **port 6379**, TLS required, cluster mode enabled.
- 7 shards × (1 primary + 1 replica), `cache.r7g.xlarge`. The seventh shard was added during INC-2025-047.
- `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu`; target memory headroom 60%.
- AUTH token: Secrets Manager `atlas/prod/redis`, key `auth_token`.
- Env var: `ATLAS_REDIS_ADDR=clustercfg.atlas-redis-prod.x7yq.use1.cache.amazonaws.com:6379`, `ATLAS_REDIS_TLS=true`, `ATLAS_REDIS_CLUSTER=true`.

Dashboard: "Atlas / Redis Overview".

documents.title: Staging Redis endpoint
documents.summary: Staging Redis is a single non-cluster ElastiCache node at atlas-redis-stg.internal on port 6380 without TLS.
documents.body:
- Endpoint: `atlas-redis-stg.internal`, **port 6380** (non-default port chosen so staging DSNs can't be pasted into prod by accident), no TLS, cluster mode **disabled**, single `cache.t4g.medium` node.
- AUTH token: Secrets Manager `atlas/staging/redis`, key `auth_token`.
- Env var: `ATLAS_REDIS_ADDR=atlas-redis-stg.internal:6380`, `ATLAS_REDIS_TLS=false`, `ATLAS_REDIS_CLUSTER=false`.

Because staging isn't in cluster mode, multi-key commands across slots work there and fail in prod with `CROSSSLOT`. Use hash tags (`rq:{lane}`) if you need multi-key operations.

documents.title: Kafka bootstrap brokers and auth per environment
documents.summary: MSK bootstrap addresses for prod, staging and local, with SASL/SCRAM on port 9096.
documents.body:
| Env | Bootstrap (first broker shown) | Port | Auth |
|---|---|---|---|
| prod | `b-1.atlasprod.kfk7c3.c3.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` (b-1…b-6) | 9096 | SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 over TLS |
| staging | `b-1.atlasstg.q2m9d1.c2.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` (b-1…b-3) | 9096 | SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 over TLS |
| dr (us-west-2) | `b-1.atlasdr.m4n8x2.c1.kafka.us-west-2.amazonaws.com` | 9096 | SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 over TLS |
| local | `localhost` (Redpanda) | 19092 | none |

Services read `ATLAS_KAFKA_BROKERS` (comma-separated) and `ATLAS_KAFKA_SASL_USER`; the password comes from the pod secret key `kafka_sasl_password`, synced from `AmazonMSK_atlas_<env>_<svc>`. Port 9094 (TLS without SASL) is disabled on all clusters.

Client settings worth knowing: producers use `acks=all` with idempotence enabled; consumers default to `auto.offset.reset=earliest` for new groups, except `tracking-ingest`, which uses `latest` because replaying 72 hours of pings for a brand-new group is never what you want. `atlasctl kafka` subcommands read the same brokers from `~/.atlasctl/config.yaml` per environment and fetch SCRAM credentials via your SSO session. Broker hostnames change if MSK replaces the cluster, so never hard-code them in code; always read `ATLAS_KAFKA_BROKERS`.

documents.title: Where secrets live: SSM Parameter Store
documents.summary: Service secrets are SecureString parameters under /atlas/<env>/<svc>/<key> in SSM, read at startup.
documents.body: Secrets are stored as SSM Parameter Store SecureStrings, one parameter per value: `/atlas/<env>/<svc>/<key>`, for example `/atlas/prod/billing-svc/pg_password` or `/atlas/prod/notify-svc/twilio_auth_token`. Each service's IRSA role may read only its own prefix. Services fetch parameters at startup via `platform/config.LoadSSM()`; changing a value requires a pod restart. KMS key alias: `alias/atlas-ssm`.

documents.title: Where secrets live: Secrets Manager via External Secrets
documents.summary: Secrets now live in AWS Secrets Manager as atlas/<env>/<svc> JSON secrets synced by External Secrets; supersedes the SSM layout.
documents.body:
Supersedes `env-secrets-ssm-parameter-store`. Migration completed 2025-08-28 (ADR-016); the `/atlas/*` SSM parameters were deleted on 2025-09-15.

- One JSON secret per service per environment: `atlas/<env>/<svc>`, e.g. `atlas/prod/billing-svc` with keys `pg_user`, `pg_password`, and any service-specific keys.
- Shared infrastructure secrets: `atlas/<env>/redis`, `atlas/<env>/pgbouncer`, `atlas/<env>/unleash`, `atlas/<env>/okta`.
- Kafka SCRAM secrets are the exception: MSK requires names prefixed `AmazonMSK_`, so they're `AmazonMSK_atlas_<env>_<svc>`.
- The External Secrets Operator (namespace `external-secrets`, `ClusterSecretStore` named `aws-secrets-manager`) syncs each into a Kubernetes Secret `<svc>-secrets` every hour.
- Postgres passwords rotate every 30 days via the `atlas-pg-rotator` Lambda. Others rotate manually.
- KMS key alias: `alias/atlas-secrets`.

No secret values are ever committed, logged, or put in `config/atlas.yaml`.

documents.title: Atlas environment variable reference
documents.summary: Complete reference of environment variables used by Atlas Go services, eta-predictor and the ops console, with defaults and per-environment values.
documents.body:
Environment variables in Atlas are for **bootstrap** values only: things a process needs before it can read its config file, plus a handful of operational overrides that must be changeable without a config deploy. Everything else belongs in `config/atlas.yaml` (see the config key reference). This memory is generated from `platform/config/env.go`, `ml/eta-predictor/app/settings.py` and `web/ops-console/src/env.ts`, then annotated by hand; if you add a variable, add it here.

Conventions: shared variables start with `ATLAS_`; service-specific ones start with the service's short name (`DISPATCH_`, `TRACKING_`, `BILLING_`, `RATES_`, `NOTIFY_`, `ETA_`); browser variables start with `VITE_` because Vite only exposes those to client code. Values below are production unless marked.

## Shared (all Go services)

| Variable | Purpose | Prod value / default |
|---|---|---|
| `ATLAS_ENV` | Environment name; selects `config/atlas.<env>.yaml` overlay | `prod` (`staging`, `dr`, `local`) |
| `ATLAS_SERVICE_NAME` | Used in logs (`svc` key), metrics and traces | set by Helm chart |
| `ATLAS_PG_DSN` | Postgres DSN assembled from secrets | `postgres://<user>:<pw>@pgbouncer.atlas.svc.cluster.local:6432/<db>?sslmode=require` |
| `ATLAS_PG_DIRECT_DSN` | Direct writer DSN for migrations and outbox-relay only | writer endpoint on 5432 |
| `ATLAS_PG_MAX_CONNS` | pgx pool size per pod | `10` |
| `ATLAS_REDIS_ADDR` | Redis endpoint | prod cluster config endpoint on 6379; staging `atlas-redis-stg.internal:6380` |
| `ATLAS_REDIS_TLS` / `ATLAS_REDIS_CLUSTER` | Redis mode | `true` / `true` in prod, `false` / `false` in staging |
| `ATLAS_KAFKA_BROKERS` | Comma-separated bootstrap list | MSK brokers on 9096 |
| `ATLAS_KAFKA_SASL_USER` | SCRAM username | `<svc>` |
| `ATLAS_KAFKA_SASL_SECRET_ARN` | ARN of the `AmazonMSK_atlas_<env>_<svc>` secret, used by atlasctl and the startup check | per service |
| `ATLAS_UNLEASH_URL` | Unleash API | `https://flags.nwf.internal/api` |
| `ATLAS_UNLEASH_TOKEN` | Server-side SDK token (from `atlas/<env>/unleash`) | secret |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | Collector address | `http://otel-collector.observability:4317` |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` | Head sampling ratio | `0.1` |
| `ATLAS_LOG_LEVEL` | slog level override | `info` (never `debug` in prod except during an incident, and revert afterwards) |
| `ATLAS_HTTP_ADDR` | HTTP listen address | `:<service port>` e.g. `:8081` |
| `ATLAS_GRPC_ADDR` | gRPC listen address | e.g. `:50051` |
| `ATLAS_METRICS_ADDR` | Prometheus metrics listener | `:9090` |
| `GOMEMLIMIT` | Go soft memory limit | 90% of the container limit (e.g. `1380MiB` for tracking-ingest's 1.5 GiB) |

## dispatch-svc

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `DISPATCH_MAX_TENDERS_PER_CARRIER` | Global default open-tender cap per carrier; exceeding it returns ATL-4012. Per-carrier overrides live in `dispatch.carrier_capacity.max_open` | `25` |
| `DISPATCH_RATE_ENGINE_ADDR` | gRPC address of rate-engine | `rate-engine.atlas.svc.cluster.local:50054` |
| `DISPATCH_RATE_DEADLINE_MS` | Deadline on quote calls | `800` |
| `DISPATCH_TENDER_EXPIRER_ENABLED` | Runs the tender-expirer loop in this pod | `true` on 2 of 8 pods (leader-elected), toggled by chart |

## tracking-svc and tracking-ingest

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `TRACKING_CONSUMER_GROUP` | Group ID for the ingest consumer | `tracking-ingest` |
| `TRACKING_INGEST_BATCH_MAX` | Max pings per COPY batch | `15000` |
| `TRACKING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_<PROVIDER>` | HMAC secrets for ELD webhooks, e.g. `TRACKING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_SAMSARA` | from `atlas/<env>/tracking-svc` |
| `TRACKING_SSE_MAX_CONNS` | Cap on SSE connections per API pod | `600` |

Note that the stale-ping threshold (15 minutes) is a config key, `tracking.ping.stale_after`, not an environment variable, despite what older docs said.

## billing-svc

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `BILLING_AUTO_FINALISE` | Whether invoices finalise automatically once a POD is present | `true` |
| `BILLING_FX_SOURCE` | FX rate source for `billing.fx_rates` | `ecb` |
| `BILLING_CLOSE_FREEZE` | Blocks non-read APIs during month-end close tooling runs | `false` |

The invoice lock timeout (5000 ms, ATL-5102) is `billing.invoice.lock_timeout_ms` in config, not an environment variable.

## rate-engine

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `RATES_DAT_API_BASE` | DAT market-data API | `https://api.dat.com/v3` (token in `atlas/prod/rate-engine`) |
| `RATES_CACHE_DISABLED` | Emergency switch to bypass Redis quote cache | `false` |

## notify-svc

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `NOTIFY_TWILIO_MESSAGING_SERVICE_SID` | Twilio messaging service for the Atlas subaccount | `MG…` (non-secret identifier) |
| `NOTIFY_SENDGRID_FROM` | Email sender | `dispatch@northwindfreight.com` |
| `NOTIFY_QUIET_HOURS` | Quiet window in driver local time | `21:00-06:00` |
| `NOTIFY_DRY_RUN` | Render and log but don't send (always `true` in staging) | `false` |

## eta-predictor (Python)

| Variable | Purpose | Prod value |
|---|---|---|
| `ETA_MODEL_URI` | MLflow model reference loaded at startup | `models:/eta-predictor/Production` (staging: `models:/eta-predictor/Staging`) |
| `ETA_SECONDARY_MODEL_URI` | Model for regions not enabled in the rollout flag | set only during regional rollouts |
| `ETA_FALLBACK_MODE` | Behaviour if the model can't load: `serve` or `fail` | `serve` in prod, `fail` in staging |
| `ETA_INFERENCE_TIMEOUT_MS` | Beyond this, fall back (ATL-5500, reason `timeout`) | `400` |
| `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` | MLflow server | `http://mlflow.nwf.internal:5000` |
| `ETA_REDIS_URL` | Feature store | `rediss://clustercfg.atlas-redis-prod.x7yq.use1.cache.amazonaws.com:6379` |
| `UVICORN_WORKERS` | Worker processes per pod | `4` |

## ops-console (build time)

| Variable | Purpose | Prod value |
|---|---|---|
| `VITE_ATLAS_API_BASE` | Gateway base URL | `https://api.northwindfreight.com` (staging: `https://api.stg.northwindfreight.com`, local: `/` proxied to `localhost:8080`) |
| `VITE_OKTA_ISSUER` | Okta authorization server | `https://northwind.okta.com/oauth2/aus1atlas` |
| `VITE_OKTA_CLIENT_ID` | SPA client ID (public, not a secret) | per environment |
| `VITE_SENTRY_DSN` | Sentry DSN for `ops-console` project | per environment |
| `VITE_ATLAS_RELEASE` | Git SHA injected by CI | build SHA |
| `VITE_MAP_TILES_URL` | Vector tile server | `https://tiles.nwf.internal/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` |

## Local development

`make dev-up` writes `.env.local` with `ATLAS_ENV=local`, `ATLAS_PG_DSN=postgres://atlas:atlas@localhost:5433/<db>?sslmode=disable`, `ATLAS_REDIS_ADDR=localhost:6379`, `ATLAS_KAFKA_BROKERS=localhost:19092` and `ETA_FALLBACK_MODE=serve`. Local Postgres is on **5433**, not 5432, so it doesn't collide with a Postgres installed on the host.

## Changing a variable in prod

Edit `deploy/envs/prod/<svc>/values.yaml` under `env:` and ship it like any other change; this creates a new ReplicaSet and goes through the canary. Don't `kubectl set env` in prod — Argo CD will revert it on the next sync (the same trap as INC-2025-027).

documents.title: Freight and logistics primer for Atlas engineers
documents.summary: A narrative glossary of the trucking and brokerage concepts that Atlas models, and where each lives in the code.
documents.body:
Northwind Freight is a freight broker with its own small asset fleet: most loads are moved by third-party carriers that Northwind contracts, and a minority by Northwind's own trucks. Atlas models the brokerage workflow. This primer explains the domain vocabulary in the order a load experiences it, with pointers to where each concept lives in the code. Individual terms also have their own short glossary memories.

## Parties

- **Shipper** — the customer who has freight to move. Pays Northwind. In code: `shipper_id`, table `dispatch.shippers`.
- **Consignee** — the receiver at the destination. Often a distribution centre (DC). Signs the proof of delivery.
- **Carrier** — the trucking company that actually moves the freight. Identified by an MC number (FMCSA operating authority), a USDOT number and usually a **SCAC** code. Northwind pays carriers. In code: `carrier_id`, `dispatch.carriers`.
- **Driver** — the person in the truck. Atlas knows drivers only through carriers and the driver app; we store a phone number for notifications and nothing else personal.
- **Broker** — Northwind itself, sitting between shipper and carrier.
- **Facility** — any place a truck stops: shipper warehouse, DC, cross-dock, port terminal, rail ramp. Facilities have a timezone (`facility_tz`), geofence radius, receiving hours and historical dwell statistics.

## The load

A **load** (sometimes "shipment" in shipper-facing UI) is one unit of freight moving from one or more pickups to one or more deliveries. Each pickup or delivery is a **stop**, in `dispatch.stops`, with a sequence number, an appointment window and a facility. The ordered stops make a **route**.

**FTL** (full truckload) loads fill a trailer for one shipper, usually one pickup and one delivery. **LTL** (less-than-truckload) loads share a trailer with other shippers' freight, with multiple stops and more handling. Atlas supports both, but pricing, ETA and billing logic differ; watch for `mode = 'LTL'` branches.

**Equipment type** matters for pricing and matching: **dry van** (the default enclosed 53' trailer), **reefer** (refrigerated, with a temperature setpoint), **flatbed** (open deck for machinery, steel, lumber), plus rarer step-deck and tanker. Equipment is one axis of the 18 ETA evaluation segments.

## Pricing

A **lane** is an origin–destination pair, in Atlas defined at 3-digit zip level (e.g. `606→303`) plus equipment. rate-engine prices lanes using **contract rates** (negotiated with a shipper for a period) or **spot rates** (market price today, from DAT market data). The price to the shipper is the **linehaul** plus a **fuel surcharge** (FSC, a per-mile amount indexed to the weekly DOE diesel price) plus any **accessorials**. The difference between what the shipper pays and what the carrier is paid is the **margin**, governed by `rates.margin_rules`.

If rate-engine has no rate data for the zip-3 pair, it returns ATL-4221 (lane not found) and a human pricer quotes manually.

## Tendering

To get a carrier, dispatch sends a **tender** — a formal offer of a specific load at a specific rate — to one carrier at a time or to a small group (a "waterfall" or "broadcast"). The carrier accepts or rejects. In EDI that's a 204 (tender) and a 990 (response). A tender left unanswered for 600 seconds expires. A **retender** is offering the load again after rejection or expiry. A carrier holding too many open tenders is refused with ATL-4012; a carrier that is suspended (lapsed insurance, safety rating, compliance hold) is refused with ATL-4013.

Some carriers find loads on a **load board** instead — a marketplace where Northwind posts available loads. Posts to external load boards are made by dispatch automatically for loads that have been retendered three times.

## Moving the freight

After acceptance, the carrier dispatches a driver. The trip to the first pickup, without freight, is **deadhead** (empty miles). Carriers hate deadhead; loads that start near where the truck is are more attractive and cheaper. A **backhaul** is a load that takes a truck back toward its home base after a delivery, which reduces the carrier's deadhead and often gets a lower rate.

During the trip, Atlas receives position data. Historically brokers relied on **check calls** — phoning the driver for location updates. Atlas replaces most check calls with GPS/ELD pings and geofences, and only generates check-call tasks for loads with no tracking signal for 2 hours.

An **ELD** (electronic logging device) is the federally mandated device recording driving hours. ELD vendors (Samsara, Motive and others) also provide GPS, which is where most tracking pings come from. **Hours of service** (HOS) rules limit driving to 11 hours in a 14-hour window with a mandatory 30-minute break after 8 hours of driving; the ETA model and the fallback rules both account for this.

A **geofence** is a virtual boundary around a facility. Entering it marks arrival, leaving marks departure. Arrival and departure times drive detention billing and the ETA model's dwell features.

## At the facility

- **Appointment** — the scheduled window to load or unload, for example 08:00–10:00 local. Some facilities are **FCFS** (first come, first served) within receiving hours.
- **Dwell time** — how long the truck was at the facility from arrival to departure. A metric, used heavily in ETA prediction.
- **Detention** — the billable part of waiting: time beyond the free time (2 hours in Northwind's standard terms) that the shipper or consignee is charged for, because the carrier's truck was held.
- **Lumper** — a third-party worker (or company) that unloads the truck at a DC, paid on the spot; the fee is later rebilled to the shipper as an accessorial with the lumper receipt as proof.
- **Layover** — when a driver has to wait overnight because a facility can't load or unload that day. Billed as a flat accessorial.
- **TONU** (truck ordered, not used) — the shipper cancels after the truck is dispatched; the carrier gets a flat fee.

## Paperwork

- **BOL** (bill of lading) — the shipping contract and receipt given at pickup, listing the freight. Uploaded to docs-svc.
- **POD** (proof of delivery) — the signed BOL or delivery receipt at the destination. Billing does not invoice automatically until a signed POD is present.
- **Rate confirmation** ("rate con") — the document sent to the carrier confirming agreed rate and terms after tender acceptance. Generated by dispatch.

## Money after delivery

When a load is delivered with a POD, billing creates an **invoice** to the shipper (accounts receivable) and a **carrier settlement** (accounts payable). **Quick pay** lets carriers get paid in 2 days instead of 30 in exchange for a 2–3% fee. All amounts are integer minor units plus currency (ADR-026). **Accessorials** (detention, lumper, layover, TONU, liftgate, inside delivery) appear as separate invoice lines.

## Performance

Carriers are rated on a **carrier scorecard**: on-time pickup and delivery percentage, tender acceptance rate, tracking compliance (share of the trip with pings), and claims. Scorecards influence which carriers get tendered first.

## Other codes you will meet

- **MC / DOT numbers** — carrier registration numbers with FMCSA.
- **SCAC** — Standard Carrier Alpha Code, 2–4 letters, the key used in EDI and by edi-bridge's partner configs.
- **Drayage** — short-distance moves of shipping containers between ports or rail ramps and nearby warehouses. A separate product line with its own facility types; Atlas supports it for port of Savannah and Los Angeles/Long Beach.
- **Cross-dock** — a facility where freight moves from inbound to outbound trucks without storage, common in LTL.
- **Hazmat** — hazardous materials, requiring certified drivers and placards; notifications about hazmat loads are sent with `urgency=URGENT`.

When in doubt about a term used in a ticket, check this primer first and then ask in #atlas-dispatch; Mei-Ling Zhou and the dispatch floor leads are happy to explain how things work in practice.

documents.title: Dwell time
documents.summary: Dwell time is the total time a truck spends at a facility between geofence arrival and departure; a metric, not a charge.
documents.body: **Dwell time**: elapsed time from confirmed geofence arrival to confirmed departure at a stop, stored as `dwell_seconds` on `tracking.stop_events` and aggregated per facility (P50/P90 over 90 days) in `tracking.facility_dwell_stats`. It is an operational metric and a key ETA feature — facilities with long median dwell push downstream ETAs later. Dwell is **not** billed; the billable portion of waiting is detention, which only starts after free time.

documents.title: Detention (detention time)
documents.summary: Detention is billable waiting time beyond two hours of free time at a facility, charged at $75/hour up to $600/day.
documents.body:
**Detention**: the portion of a truck's wait at a facility beyond the free time, which Northwind charges the shipper and passes (partly) to the carrier. Northwind standard terms: 2 hours free from the later of appointment start or arrival, then $75 per hour billed in 15-minute increments, capped at $600 per stop per day. Contract customers may have different terms in `billing.customer_terms`.

Detention is computed by billing-svc from the same geofence arrival/departure events used for dwell time, so dwell ≥ detention + free time. If arrival events are late or missing (for example after a tracking lag incident), detention cannot be billed automatically and the stop goes to the exceptions queue. Detention appears on the invoice as accessorial code `DET`.

Worked example: appointment 08:00–10:00, truck arrives 07:40, departs 12:25. Free time runs from 08:00 (the later of appointment start and arrival) to 10:00; billable detention is 10:00–12:25, rounded to 2.5 hours, so $187.50. The dwell time for the same stop is 4 h 45 min. Carrier-side detention pay follows the carrier's rate confirmation and is usually $50/hour.

documents.title: Tender
documents.summary: A tender is a formal offer of a specific load at a specific rate to a carrier, which the carrier accepts or rejects.
documents.body: **Tender**: dispatch's offer of a load to a carrier. Lives in `dispatch.tenders` with states DRAFT, OFFERED, ACCEPTED, REJECTED, EXPIRED, WITHDRAWN. Offers expire after 600 seconds. In EDI, the tender is a 204 and the response a 990. Not to be confused with a "quote", which is only a price from rate-engine with no carrier attached, or a "load board post", which is open to any carrier.

documents.title: Lane
documents.summary: A lane is an origin-destination pair (zip-3 to zip-3) plus equipment type, the unit rate-engine prices.
documents.body: **Lane**: origin zip-3 → destination zip-3 plus equipment, written like `606→303 VAN`. The Redis quote key uses it: `rq:{lane}:{equipment}`. Contract rates are negotiated per lane per shipper; spot rates come from DAT. A missing lane returns ATL-4221. "Lane density" means how many loads Northwind moves on a lane per week; dense lanes get better carrier rates.

documents.title: Deadhead and backhaul
documents.summary: Deadhead is empty miles driven without freight; a backhaul is a load that returns a truck toward home and reduces deadhead.
documents.body:
**Deadhead**: miles a truck drives empty, typically from its last delivery to the next pickup. Atlas computes `deadhead_miles` for each tender from the truck's last known position (or the carrier's domicile) to the first pickup; dispatch ranks carriers partly by it.

**Backhaul**: a load that brings a truck back toward its home base. Carriers accept lower rates for backhauls because the alternative is deadhead. rate-engine applies a backhaul discount (`rates.margin_rules.backhaul_adjustment`) when a carrier's domicile is within 150 miles of the destination.

documents.title: Bill of lading (BOL)
documents.summary: The BOL is the shipping contract and receipt issued at pickup, stored by docs-svc.
documents.body: **BOL (bill of lading)**: the document the shipper hands the driver at pickup describing the freight (pieces, weight, class, hazmat) and acting as the contract of carriage. Atlas stores BOL images in docs-svc with `doc_type = 'BOL'`. The BOL number is often the shipper's primary reference and is searchable in the console. Not the same as the POD, although a signed BOL frequently serves as the POD.

documents.title: Proof of delivery (POD)
documents.summary: The POD is the consignee-signed delivery receipt; billing will not invoice automatically without a signed POD.
documents.body: **POD (proof of delivery)**: the delivery receipt signed by the consignee, usually a signed copy of the BOL. Drivers upload a photo through the driver app to docs-svc (`doc_type = 'POD'`). Textract checks for a signature; a POD without one sends the load to the billing exceptions queue. "POD received" is the event that lets billing-svc finalise an invoice when `BILLING_AUTO_FINALISE=true`.

documents.title: Reefer
documents.summary: A reefer is a refrigerated trailer with a temperature setpoint; reefer loads have stricter appointment and monitoring rules.
documents.body: **Reefer**: refrigerated trailer. Reefer loads carry a setpoint (e.g. 34°F) and continuous-temperature requirement stored in `dispatch.loads.temp_setpoint_f`. Cold-storage DCs typically have strict receiving windows, so a reefer load arriving just after the window may not be unloaded until the next day — a pattern the ETA model has to learn, and the one implicated in INC-2026-019. Reefer temperature telemetry arrives from ELD providers alongside GPS pings.

documents.title: FTL vs LTL
documents.summary: FTL is a full trailer for one shipper; LTL shares a trailer across shippers with multiple stops.
documents.body:
**FTL (full truckload)**: one shipper's freight fills or reserves the trailer; usually one pickup and one delivery; priced per mile on the lane.

**LTL (less-than-truckload)**: several shippers' freight shares a trailer, with multiple stops and often cross-docking; priced by weight, freight class and distance. In Atlas, `loads.mode` is `FTL` or `LTL`. A truck may carry several LTL loads at once, which is why telemetry is keyed by `truck_id` rather than `load_id`.

documents.title: Accessorial charges
documents.summary: Accessorials are extra charges beyond linehaul and fuel, such as detention, lumper, layover, TONU and liftgate.
documents.body: **Accessorials**: services or events beyond the basic move, billed as separate invoice lines with codes: `DET` detention, `LUM` lumper, `LAY` layover, `TONU` truck ordered not used, `LFT` liftgate, `INS` inside delivery, `RDL` redelivery. Each requires evidence (geofence times for detention, receipts for lumper). Amounts come from `billing.customer_terms` or standard terms. Carrier-side accessorials are settled separately and can differ from the shipper-side charge.

documents.title: Lumper fee
documents.summary: A lumper fee pays third-party unloaders at a warehouse; it is rebilled to the shipper with the receipt.
documents.body: **Lumper**: a third-party worker or service that unloads a truck at a DC. The driver often pays on the spot (via Comchek or card) and uploads the lumper receipt to docs-svc (`doc_type = 'LUMPER_RECEIPT'`). Billing adds a `LUM` accessorial to the shipper invoice and reimburses the carrier. Without a receipt, the charge is held for manual review.

documents.title: Drayage
documents.summary: Drayage is short-haul movement of shipping containers between ports or rail ramps and nearby facilities.
documents.body: **Drayage**: moving intermodal containers short distances, e.g. from the Port of Savannah to a warehouse 40 miles away. Drayage loads in Atlas have `mode = 'DRAY'` and reference a container number and chassis. Special events: **per diem** (charges for keeping a container too long) and **demurrage** (charges for leaving it at the terminal). Atlas currently supports drayage at Savannah and LA/Long Beach.

documents.title: Check call
documents.summary: A check call is a manual status update from a driver; Atlas creates check-call tasks only for loads without tracking.
documents.body: **Check call**: the traditional practice of calling a driver to ask where they are. Atlas generates a check-call task in the console only when a load has had no tracking signal (GPS/ELD ping or EDI 214) for 2 hours while in transit. Completed check calls are recorded as a low-confidence position with `source=CHECK_CALL`.

documents.title: Geofence
documents.summary: A geofence is a circular boundary around a facility; two consecutive pings inside it confirm arrival.
documents.body: **Geofence**: a circle around a facility (default radius 400 m, `tracking.geofence.default_radius_m`, overridable per facility for large DCs or ports). Arrival requires two consecutive pings inside the circle; departure requires two consecutive pings outside. Geofence events are the basis for dwell time, detention and stop status in the console.

documents.title: ETA confidence band
documents.summary: The ETA confidence band is the P10–P90 range from the eta-tft model, shown in the console and used for late-delivery warnings.
documents.body:
**ETA confidence band**: since the v4 transformer model (ADR-024), each prediction includes P10, P50 and P90 arrival estimates. The console shows P50 as the ETA and draws the P10–P90 range as a shaded band on the load timeline. Dispatch uses **P90** to decide whether to warn a shipper that a delivery is at risk: if P90 is later than the appointment end, a "delivery at risk" notification is queued.

The band is hidden whenever the prediction came from the rules-based fallback (`source: fallback`, ATL-5500), because the fallback has no calibrated uncertainty. Wide bands (P90 − P50 over 4 hours) signal an uncertain prediction; there is work in progress to suppress shipper notifications in that case.

Shipper-facing messages quote only P50 rounded to 15 minutes. The GBM model before April 2026 produced a point estimate only, so older screenshots have no band.

In the API, the fields are `eta_p50`, `eta_p10` and `eta_p90` (RFC 3339 instants) on the load's `eta` object, plus `p10_minutes`/`p90_minutes` offsets on eta-api's own `/v1/predict` response.

documents.title: Carrier scorecard
documents.summary: The carrier scorecard rates carriers on on-time performance, tender acceptance, tracking compliance and claims.
documents.body:
**Carrier scorecard**: a weekly computed rating per carrier, stored in `dispatch.carrier_scorecards` and shown in the console's Carriers area. Components and weights:

- On-time pickup (20%) and on-time delivery (30%), measured against appointment windows using geofence events.
- Tender acceptance rate (20%): accepted ÷ offered over 30 days. Rejections with reason `NO_CAPACITY` count half.
- Tracking compliance (20%): share of in-transit time with at least one ping every 15 minutes.
- Claims (10%): cargo damage/loss claims per 100 loads.

Scores range 0–100. Carriers below 60 drop to the end of tender waterfalls; carriers above 90 are "preferred" and get first look. Scores are recomputed Mondays at 05:00 UTC by the `scorecard-weekly` job. A suspended carrier (ATL-4013) keeps its score but receives no tenders.

Tracking gaps caused by Atlas itself (for example the INC-2025-031 lag window) are excluded from tracking compliance by the `scorecard_exclusion_windows` table, which the incident commander fills in after a tracking incident.

documents.title: ATL-4012: carrier open-tender capacity exceeded
documents.summary: ATL-4012 means the carrier already holds the maximum number of open tenders; it is not a suspension.
documents.body: **ATL-4012 — carrier capacity exceeded.** Returned by dispatch-svc (HTTP 409) when offering a tender would push the carrier's open (`OFFERED`) tenders above its limit: `DISPATCH_MAX_TENDERS_PER_CARRIER` (default 25) or the per-carrier `max_open` override. It is transient: once tenders are accepted, rejected or expire, the carrier can receive new ones. Frequently confused with ATL-4013. INC-2025-036 produced false ATL-4012s when expired tenders didn't release capacity. `details` includes `carrier_id`, `limit` and `open_tenders`.

documents.title: ATL-4013: carrier suspended
documents.summary: ATL-4013 means the carrier is suspended (insurance lapse, safety or compliance hold) and cannot be tendered at all.
documents.body: **ATL-4013 — carrier suspended.** Returned by dispatch-svc (HTTP 422) when the target carrier's status is `SUSPENDED`. Causes: insurance certificate expired (automatic, from the Highway integration), FMCSA authority revoked, safety rating unsatisfactory, or a manual compliance hold by carrier ops. It persists until the cause is cleared — waiting doesn't help. `details` includes `carrier_id` and `suspension_reason`. Don't confuse it with ATL-4012, which is only a temporary tender-count limit.

documents.title: SCAC code
documents.summary: A SCAC is the 2–4 letter Standard Carrier Alpha Code that identifies carriers in EDI and in edi-bridge partner configs.
documents.body: **SCAC (Standard Carrier Alpha Code)**: a 2–4 letter code assigned by NMFTA identifying a carrier, e.g. `RDWY`, `ODFL`. edi-bridge keys partner configs (`partners/<scac>.yaml`) and the `edi.inbound.v1` topic by SCAC. Not every small carrier has one; for those Atlas uses the MC number as the identifier and they cannot integrate over EDI.
